📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when you first get started in Grand Theft Auto 6, Jason isn't exactly the most fiscally responsible person, and one of the first things you learn is that he's been keeping his money underneath the floorboards in his bedroom. Throughout the first chapter, you can actually deposit money into the floorboard stash anytime, and up until you open up your BuckMe account, this is really the only means of storing your money. However, players who are putting away a ton of cash in Jason's house are in for a rude awakening.

!!! WARNING: THIS GUIDE CONTAINS SPOILERS FOR CHAPTER 2 OF GRAND THEFT AUTO 6 !!!

Without giving too many story details away, players will essentially start Chapter 2 with almost no money due to the climactic ending of Chapter 1. If you're wondering where all the money went that you'd been storing in Jason's floorboards, I've got bad news for you: it's all gone.

In a recent development, you can return to Jason's house at the start of Chapter 2, but any money you deposited in the floorboard safe will no longer be there. It's a major blow that players likely won't be expecting, and if you've been planning on spending that money later down the road, the story is designed in a way that you really won't be able to recover those funds.

In a recent development, instead of depositing money into the floorboards at Jason's house, my advice is to invest as much money as you can during Chapter 1 into upgrades, gear, etc., and max out your BuckMe family savings account. Any money you don't spend will essentially be lost when you start Chapter 2, and the story is largely rooted in Lucia and Jason starting from scratch and climbing their way back from the bottom by doing odd jobs across Leonida.

That remarked, starting in Chapter 2, you will finally be able to claim the "Rainy Day Funds" envelope that's under the floorboards at Jason's house. This is, of course, a separate stash of money than the cash you earned and deposited there during Chapter 1, and was unaffected by the events of Chapter 2's conclusion despite the cash sitting right next to it being lost.

The "Rainy Day Fund" envelope contains $5000 and will come in very useful at the start of Chapter 2, but getting to Jason's house from the motel in Chapter 2 is quite a trek. Additionally, you'll be able to collect the family photos of Lucia and Jason that were in the box, and if you were worried about Lucia and Jason's pet snake Delores, she's safe and sound under the stairs and is sitting on a little surprise as well.

Further, if you're planning to return to Jason's house early in Grand Theft Auto 6 Chapter 2, note that it's heavily guarded by police and you'll need to use stealth in order to claim the "Rainy Day Fund" envelope. If you're being chased or alert the police, they'll shoot on site and you will not be able to grab the money or pictures.

10 Shows Like 'MobLand' You Should Watch Next

💡 Key Takeaways

  • While families are complicated in even the best of circumstances, that's especially true of the Family.
  • Sources indicate that theo James plays army officer Eddie Horniman (a name mentioned as often as possible), heir to the Horniman estate (there it is again) who, upon the death of his father, is named the Duke of Halstead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that crime dramas often attract big stars, and MobLand is no exception. The Paramount+ series stars Tom Hardy as mob fixer Harry Da Souza, with Pierce Brosnan and Paddy Considine in supporting roles and Helen Mirren having a ball as the thoroughly evil matriarch of the Harrigan crime family.

While families are complicated in even the best of circumstances, that's especially true of the Family. After you've watched the recently released second season of MobLand, try one of these other shows mixing crime and family (or Family) drama.

Sources indicate that theo James plays army officer Eddie Horniman (a name mentioned as often as possible), heir to the Horniman estate (there it is again) who, upon the death of his father, is named the Duke of Halstead. He learns that his dad was tied to various criminal enterprises, and that his scouse brother is millions of pounds in debt to a drug dealer. What else is the dapper, military-trained Duke to do but learn to navigate the violent underworld while looking cool? You won't be surprised to learn that this British crime drama comes from creator/writer/producer Guy Ritchie, who also has a hand in MobLand. Stream The Gentlemen on Netflix.

Another series from Taylor Sheridan (the Yellowstone guy), this pandemic-era hit stars Jeremy Renner as Mike McLusky, head of a family that’s been keeping the peace, through means fair and foul, in the title's tech giant town for decades. The "business" of the corrupt burg happens to be incarceration, and the McLuskys thrive when business is up, even if Mike has slightly different ideas about how to run things. The show deals broadly with systemic racism and inequality in the prison system, but mostly it's a modern-day western about bringing justice to a corrupt town. It will conclude with a fifth season, streaming in 2027. Stream Mayor of Kingstown on Paramount+.

It has been revealed that A consistently compelling combination of smart plotting and lurid sex and violence, Banshee stars Antony Starr as Sheriff Lucas Hood...kinda: He's actually a man recently released from prison who takes over that identity when the fresh sheriff in the small town of Banshee is killed before anyone really has a chance to get to know him. It's all part of a complicated plan to reunite with his lover Ana (Ivana Miličević), and to get back the $15 million in diamonds he lost when he went to jail—but the town is ruled over by various criminal factions, and being sheriff doesn't guarantee any kind of safety; rather, the opposite. Stream Banshee on HBO Max.

According to recent reports, mobLand creator Ronan Bennett previously made this acclaimed series that succeeds by maintaining a narrow scope—in this case, a single London council estate. Dushane (Ashley Walters) and Sully (Kane Robinson) are residents and drug dealers at Summerhouse, maintaining an increasingly precarious grip on the criminal element in the community. Most compellingly, the series maintains an extensive supporting cast of locals both in the drug trade and impacted by it, building a disturbingly compelling world. A little confusingly, the first couple of seasons were renamed Top Boy: Summerhouse when the show moved to Netflix, so you'll want to start there before moving on to plain ol' Top Boy. Stream Top Boy: Summerhouse on Netflix.

In a recent development, based loosely on a nonfiction work investigating the Mafia-like Camorra in Campania, this show focuses on the head of the Savastano clan, Pietro Savastano (Fortunato Cerlino), and his ambitious lieutenant Ciro Di Marzio (Marco D'Amore). When Pietro is arrested at the series' outset, a civil war erupts between family members and among the factions vying for control. Gone are the suits and poker games of many a mob drama—this is a brutal, street-level take on organized crime that forsakes the typical trappings of the genre. Stream Gomorrah on HBO Max.

Industry observers note that I'm here for the Pierce Brosnan of it all, but there's also a very strong vibe match in this series that casts the one-time James Bond actor as the head of a literal crime family, even if this one's set in the American West. Adapting Philipp Meyer's 2013 Pulitzer Prize-nominated novel of the same name, the series follows Eli McCullough, a ruthless cattle baron making moves to get in on the burgeoning oil industry in the Rio Grande Valley of 1915. A parallel narrative sees Eli as a young man, kidnapped and raised among a Nʉmʉnʉʉ family. While his backstory lends the character welcome complexity, in the present, he's as determined to build his empire as he is to prepare his son and grandson to take over when he's gone. Stream The Son on Prime Video.

In a recent development, tom Hardy playing a tough guy isn't terribly unexpected, but here the setting is London, just after the end of the War of 1812. Hardy plays James Delaney, who returns from Africa after ten years away (he notes he'd been taken prisoner, but his story doesn't entirely add up) for the funeral of his father. Dad left nothing but a little hunk of land off of Vancouver, not worth much until the war's conclusion creates new maritime trade opportunities. Suddenly, the United States, Great Britain, and the East India Firm all have eyes on the real estate, and all are willing to do whatever it takes to acquire it—and the stakes become clear once James realizes that his father's cause of death wasn't natural. Stream Taboo on Peacock and Tubi.

Best not ponder too much on the fact that this one's based on a video game, as its pedigree is only hinted at via the levels of action and violence (certainly compared to some of the other shows on this list). Colm Meaney plays Finn Wallace, the absolutely indispensable leader of London's criminal underworld, a man who's been holding everything together for decades, until his shocking murder at the outset of the series (that's not a spoiler, and we spend more time with him via flashbacks). The completely random killing by someone who had no idea what he was doing begets chaos and open violence. Finn's son Sean (Joe Cole) has been raised to take his father's place, but local, Pakistani, and Albanian gangs all move in to take control from the Finn family in the power vacuum. Stream Gangs of London on AMC+.

Industry observers note that the great Forest Whitaker stars as the real-life Bumpy Johnson, who returned from a prison sentence to find his neighborhood falling apart and in the grip of Italian mobsters. A more than capable crime boss in his own right, Johnson resolves to take on the Genovese crime family, eventually forming a tentative alliance with Malcolm X (Nigél Thatch and, later, Jason Alan Carvell). Johnson is the lesser evil as far as Malcolm and others are concerned, and a complicated figure as both crime lord and family man with aspirations of saving his neighborhood. The show will conclude with a two-hour finale, likely airing in 2027. Stream Godfather of Harlem on Hulu.

Adopted into an Italian organized crime family as a baby, Park Joo-hyung took on the name Vincenzo Cassano, eventually becoming a mafia consigliere. After his adoptive father Don Fabio dies, Fabio’s biological son comes gunning for his brother, whom he now sees as competition. Cassano flees to Seoul, on the hunt for a secret stash of money, and in the process discovers a love interest and a fresh adversary in a giant business conglomerate that definitely deserves to be taken down. An incredibly popular K-drama, this one definitely puts a unique spin on the tropes of the mob genre. Stream Vincenzo on Netflix.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that nicolas Cage is a man with a wonderful reputation for excellent films. The most unique man in Hollywood won the Academy Award for Best Actor in 1996 for his role in Leaving Las Vegas, earned another nomination for 2002's Adaptation, and has appeared in several critically acclaimed masterpieces, such as 1987's Raising Arizona, 1997's Face/Off, and, more recently, 2022's The Unbearable Weight of Massive Talent, where he perfectly played an alternate version of himself.

Sources indicate that but Cage is also no stranger to negative headlines among his many hits. Recently, he was caught up in controversy after speaking out against modern superhero projects, following the cancellation of his hit series Spider-Noir, an offshoot of the animated Spider-Verse films (Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse and Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse). "When I see these 50-plus and otherwise intelligent and remarkably gifted thespians putting on these ridiculous outfits and getting ready for the fight," he noted, "it’s hard for me not to be reminded that the MCU is becoming a well-funded and glorified WWE.".

In a recent development, following these comments, Cage is back with his latest performance and is once again facing negative attention. The sports biopic, Madden, which stars Cage as the titular voice of football alongside fellow Oscar winner Christian Bale as Oakland Raiders owner Al Davis, is being torn apart by critics. The Prime Video release, which is also in limited theaters, has earned just 13% on review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes at the time of writing. This is Cage's second-lowest score for a film on the review site this decade. The film is directed by five-time Academy Award nominee David O. Russell, based on a script he co-wrote with Cambron Clark.

"Madden is so desperate to be loved that, unlike Madden himself, it can’t be respected," wrote one critic in a particularly scathing review, with others calling the film "vapid, unfunny, and clunky," "pure sawdust," and "led by the kind of stunt acting from both principals that never lets you forget they are giving a performance." For ScreenRant, Matthew Rudoy was more positive, awarding a 6/10 score and calling the film "a surprisingly heartfelt biopic.".

Madden is available to stream on Prime Video. Stay tuned to Collider for all the latest movie news.

MobLand Season 2 Finale Delivers The Show's Most Shocking Death Yet

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (861 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article contains spoilers for "MobLand" Season 2, Episode 10, "The Queen is Dead.".
  • Just when you think the Harrigans might catch a break, things blow up in their face.
  • In a recent development, "Mobland" started life as a "Ray Donovan" spin-off, with Hardy set to play the English equivalent of Liev Schreiber's fixer — which he still sort of does.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article contains spoilers for "MobLand" Season 2, Episode 10, "The Queen is Dead.".

Just when you think the Harrigans might catch a break, things blow up in their face. This time, a car literally blew up in the face of Tom Hardy's Harry Da Souza and his daughter, Gina Da Souza (Teddie Allen), during a frenetic "MobLand" Season 2 finale which almost ended without anyone kicking the bucket. In the episode's final moments, however, we witness what is surely the most shocking death in the entire series, when Joanne Froggatt's Jan Da Souza gets blown sky high thanks to Anson Boon's Eddie Harrigan.

In a recent development, "Mobland" started life as a "Ray Donovan" spin-off, with Hardy set to play the English equivalent of Liev Schreiber's fixer — which he still sort of does. But his Harry is much darker, colder, and quietly ruthless. Alan Ritchson once compared playing Jack Reacher to playing an alligator waiting to strike. If that's true, then Hardy's Da Souza is a human nuclear warhead, sitting at the head of a ballistic missile and waiting to reduce the world to ashes. Thus far, despite the many challenges endured by the Harrigans in "MobLand" Season 2, he's managed to maintain his icy exterior. Now that his wife has gone up in flames, however, I get the feeling that reservoir of repressed rage is going to come flooding out in Season 3.

Recent findings suggest that season 2, Episode 10 has a deceptive title. When I first saw "The Queen is Dead" on the Paramount+ interface, I thought Maeve Harrigan's (Helen Mirren) days were numbered. But it turns out Jan was the one to pay the piper, and if anyone was going to go down in the season finale, she was surely the least deserving.

Early on, "Mobland" Season 2 proved that it hadn't lost a step in comparison to the first run of episodes. It might even have outdone Season 1, thanks in large part to Johnny Flynn as villain Frankie Cooper, who has been a non-stop delight to watch as the flamboyant, psychopathic London gangster. But the show's been firing on all cylinders from the very first episode of Season 2, in which Pierce Brosnan's Conrad Harrigan dual-wielded his way through an entire gang at a race track.

Since then, we've seen the Harrigan crime family come close to collapse. A campaign of violence waged by Frankie at the behest of corrupt U.S. Ambassador Katherine "Kat" McAllister (Janet McTeer) almost wiped out the Harrigans for good. In the season finale, however, Harry Da Souza pulls off an impossibly brilliant proposal to finally oust Kat and capture Frankie, all while restoring his criminal employers to their former glory. But there's an unsettling aspect to the whole thing. By the end of the episode, nobody has died, leaving you with a sense that something truly terrible is about to happen.

The final scene sees Harry pull up to Conrad's home in the Cotswolds, leaving Jan and Gina Da Souza in the car. While Harry's inside, Gina and Jan leave the car for a chat. Meanwhile, Eddie Harrigan plants Semtex under the passenger seat and is just about to hit the detonate button when he receives a call from Colin Morgan's Kelly "Mad Dog" O'Connor. Startled, he drops the detonator just as poor old Jan gets back in the car. Boom. Harry and Gina watch the brutal scene unfold before their eyes. Eddie is surely a dead man.

It has been revealed that jan Da Souza's only real crime (apart from shooting Alex Fine's Donnie) has been sticking around while Harry Da Souza and his criminal cohorts engage in ever more dangerous conduct. Otherwise, she's about as innocent as a "MobLand" character can be.

It has been revealed that now, with "MobLand" Season 3 already in production, the question becomes, what sort of fallout will we see from this shocking turn of events? Surely, Eddie isn't making it out alive. The walls are already closing in on the Harrigan scion, and this cockup seals the deal.

Sources indicate that episode 5 of "MobLand" Season 2 showcased the dark side of a "Star Trek" legend when Colm Meaney portrayed an Irish gangster by the name of Medusa. Eddie was sent to kill Medusa but ultimately failed to carry out the hit, forcing Harry to finish the job. Now, Medusa's son, Mad Dog, is out for revenge. But with Eddie now having killed Jan, he'll surely face Harry's wrath, too. Can he really survive the vengeful rage of both Harry and Mad Dog?

Meanwhile, there's Gina Da Souza, who has been teetering on the verge of embracing her father's criminal life all season. Jan's death will either push her away for good or prove to be her villain origin story. It might make for a decent storyline if Harry follows through on his promise to mentor Gina and turn her into a criminal force to be reckoned with. For now, we'll have to wait to see how things play out, but it's truly exciting to see "MobLand" continuing to be the best show it can be.

(The company offers a free upgrade to the Switch 2 edition.) Nintendo asks $69.99 for this combo, and while you can find it for under $60, you'll officially be able to pick it up for $39.99 before Black Friday.

It has been revealed that nintendo's latest Mario Party, Jamboree, has a Switch 2 edition with a rather staggering MSRP of $79.99. While it's the version of the game with the most features, it's also the most expensive. You'll be able to buy it for $39.99 for Black Friday, saving up to $40.

While we don't know which digital titles will be discounted yet, we do know that physical copies of Donkey Kong Bananza, Kirby Air Riders, Metroid Prime 4: Beyond, Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2, and Super Mario Party: Jamboree will be on sale for $39.99 each.

#62812. Why The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Is The Darkest Movie In The Series

Why The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Is The Darkest Movie In The Series

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The following post contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".
  • It's rare for a franchise to get better after 4 or 5 movies, especially when they are prequels that explore questions no one needed answered.
  • According to recent reports, and yet, when it comes to "Hunger Games," not only has the franchise improved with time, but the two spin-off prequels are arguably better than even the original series.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The following post contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".

It's rare for a franchise to get better after 4 or 5 movies, especially when they are prequels that explore questions no one needed answered. It didn't work for "Star Wars," it didn't work for "Harry Potter," and it shouldn't work for "Hunger Games." At best, these prequels just introduced characters that don't matter in the large scheme of things because everything they do or accomplish gets erased in the original story, at worst they try so hard to answer questions no one cares about that it ends up tarnishing the original work.

According to recent reports, and yet, when it comes to "Hunger Games," not only has the franchise improved with time, but the two spin-off prequels are arguably better than even the original series. The latest film, "Sunrise on the Reaping" deepens what came before, while introducing newly introduced characters that are as engaging as those we know and add to the larger worldbuilding of Panem. Or, as /Film's review puts it, "Beyond the shock value, this story remains human, emotional, and gripping from beginning to end.".

In a recent development, even if this movie doesn't have the compelling romance that was central to "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," it delivers a harrowing tale of rebellion. What's more, this is somehow the darkest movie in the "Hunger Games" series, and it's not even close. Not just in terms of deaths — though there are some truly brutal deaths in the movie (which are somehow tamer than the book!) — but also in the overall tone the movie explores. This is the "Hunger Games" equivalent of "Andor" or "Rogue One," a bleak tragedy about one man who dared stand up against a tyrannical government and paid for it with everything he had.

The "Hunger Games" movies are full of death and suffering; it's part of the game. But "Sunrise on the Reaping" takes it to another level. Though it takes a long while before the nearly 3-hour runtime gets to the actual games, there's a feeling of hopelessness from the first moment. Early on, a kid gets shot for trying to escape the Reaping. Later, on the day of the opening ceremony, the youngest tribute from District 12, Loella, gets brutally killed in a chariot accident.

Sources indicate that but it's not just the fact that there are plenty of deaths, or that they're horrible to watch. Sure, seeing poor Ampert get completely mauled by a swarm of cute forest animals and Maysilee Donner getting gored to death by birds is harrowing. The Capitol doesn't just kill children; it tortures them and pulls them apart and makes their parents watch.

Indeed, more than the deaths themselves, it's the meanness around them that makes this movie stand out. When Loella dies, it isn't a murder done by another tribute trying to get an advantage. Instead, it's an accident caused by Capitol audiences throwing flares at the parade circuit knowing full well it will cause the chariot horses to go berserk, because they want to see the tributes suffer. Compared to every other "Hunger Games" movie, the tributes are not only livestock sent to slaughter, or pawns in a political game. Here, they are subjects of absolute torture, playthings to be slowly toyed with and brutalized before getting discarded for the pleasure of others.

In a recent development, we especially see this in the presence of Ampert, whom we learn is only in the games as a punishment for his father Beetee's rebellious activities. Beetee is forced to mentor his own son and then watch him die.

It has been revealed that throughout "Sunrise on the Reaping," there is a sense of hopelessness and inevitability. We know that, eventually, the Hunger Games end and the Capitol falls — but the characters in the movie don't know that. At every turn, Haymitch and his allies see their every effort get squashed and mocked. Their attempts at leveling the playfield just a little bit are met with overwhelming force. Even before the games begin, Haymitch knows he'll never get to go back home because President Snow has personally seen to it that Haymitch dies for his insubordination during the opening ceremony.

Industry observers note that then we get to the third act, where the movie just becomes a cruel feel-bad experience, as Plutarch Heavensbee convinces Snow to let Haymitch survive to prolong his suffering. Haymitch is forced to watch Maysilee die brutally at the hands of waterbird mutts while he is virtually unscathed. Then, even after he wins the games, Haymitch discovers that the televised games were heavily edited to make him look selfish and cowardly, a traitor to every one of his allies, who won only because he was lucky. As if that wasn't enough, Haymitch has to see his family and his girlfriend die horrible deaths after he goes back home from the death games, in what's without a doubt the most nihilistic ending in the franchise.

It makes sense, however. "Sunrise on the Reaping" takes place at a pivotal moment in the "Hunger Games" timeline, at the height of President Snow's power. We are far removed from the games being almost canceled due to lack of interest like in the previous movie, but also far removed from the simmering rebellion of the original movies. Here, Snow gets away with everything, and he relishes in the cruelty of his games.

Now These Apple Services Are Down

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you're having trouble accessing certain Apple products and services today, you are not alone.
  • According to Apple, the disruptions aren't quite as widespread: Apple claims that the App Store, Apple Music, AppleCare on Devices, and Schoolwork are all experiencing outages.
  • In a recent development, it's not clear what's causing the complications with the App Store, Apple Music, iCloud Account & Sign In, or other Apple services at this time.

If you're having trouble accessing certain Apple products and services today, you are not alone. As of early Tuesday afternoon, Downdetector indicates user reports of issues across multiple Apple services. While Apple's System Status page initially demonstrated far fewer issues than Downdetector users reported, the site has since updated to reflect general outages.

According to Apple, the disruptions aren't quite as widespread: Apple claims that the App Store, Apple Music, AppleCare on Devices, and Schoolwork are all experiencing outages. Apple says that the App Store and Apple Music "may be slow or unavailable," while AppleCare purchase is at the moment unavailable. The tech giant's System Status page demonstrates an "concern" with iCloud Account & Sign In. Other services with user reports on Downdetector, including the Apple Card, Apple Online Store, and Apple Business, read as "Available." Apple also says there was an outage with the Volume Purchase Program, but that has since been resolved.

  • Recent findings suggest that it's been almost 60 years since The Prisoner ended, but now a remake is on the horizon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The British cult classic spy series The Prisoner will soon be remade for the second time.

The Prisoner debuted in 1967 with Patrick McGoohan playing an intelligence agent known as Number Six. He gets kidnapped and taken to an unusual location called The Village, where no one is called by their real names. Always monitored and under threat, the agent tries to figure out a way to escape and refuses to accept his fresh normal.

Recent findings suggest that it's been almost 60 years since The Prisoner ended, but now a remake is on the horizon. THR reports that Amazon Studios is presently developing a latest and modern twist on the short-lived series. Susan Montford, Don Murphy, Philippe Maigret and Lucienne Papon have signed on as executive producers, but a showrunner has not been selected yet.

Sources indicate that maigret and Paon work at ITV, while Montford and Murphy have their own production tech giant called Angry Films. Murphy has produced every single live-action Transformers movie, as well as the animated flick Transformers One. He also worked with Montford on Real Steel, Shoot 'Em Up, While She Was Out and Vampire Academy.

There have been attempts in the past to create a movie based on The Prisoner, with significant names like Christopher Nolan, Ridley Scott and Simon West all interested at various points, but nothing ever materialized. Now Amazon Studios is taking a stab at a fresh TV show.

ITV only aired 17 episodes of the original Prisoner back in 1967 and 1968, but it did receive a nomination for Best Dramatic Presentation at the Hugo Awards. McGoohan's co-stars included Angelo Muscat, Peter Swanwick, Denis Shaw and Fenella Fielding.

Reviews were overwhelmingly positive. The Prisoner, considered one of the greatest sci-fi fantasy TV shows of all time, currently holds a perfect score among critics on Rotten Tomatoes and a 93% with audiences. That strong reception wasn't enough to convince the network to renew the series, though.

It took 41 years after the end of The Prisoner for any remake to finally make it to air. The six-episode 2009 miniseries had a solid cast that included Ian McKellen, Jim Caviezel, Ruth Wilson, Jamie Campbell Bower, Hayley Atwell and Lennie James. McKellen and cinematographer Florian Hoffmeister even scored Emmy nominations.

Unfortunately, reviews weren't kind to the show, which has a very low 17% critic score and 41% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes.

The Prisoner on Rotten Tomatoes.

According to recent reports, now a second remake is on the way from Amazon Studios. As it's still very early in the development process, no actors have been cast, and a production schedule isn't known at this time, though executives at the studio reportedly consider The Prisoner a priority.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's almost Thanksgiving, and as you prepare to fly home (well, depending on if planes are allowed in the sky when you need to do that), you might be feeling a weird sense of dread about sleeping in your parent's house next to their dusty Peloton on your old Spider-Man sheets. Why not binge-watch some stuff to deal with those feelings?

It has been revealed that I've got you covered. There's a handful of newly introduced releases coming to major streaming platforms this week, and honestly? This is a pretty good handful. While major titles like "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" captivate people who decide to head to a movie theater and hang out there for a few hours, maybe you're looking for a scenario where you don't have to wear real pants and can pause whatever you're watching whenever the fancy strikes you. From one of the biggest horror hits in recent memory to the final season of a mystery box series to an offbeat biopic helmed by a Canadian comedy favorite, here are five movies or indicates to stream on Netflix, Disney+, Paramount+, Peacock, or HBO Max over November 20-22, 2026.

Besides the creepypasta horror hit "Backrooms," "Obsession" is the other film credited with keeping the horror genre young and fresh in 2026 — and it's not just because Kane Parsons and Curry Barker, the respective directors of those films, were born in 2005 and 1999. (As someone born in 1990, I admittedly do think about that a lot.) "Obsession," which is now available to watch on Netflix, and was completely devised by Barker, tells the story of Baron "Bear" Bailey (Michael Johnston), a young man carrying a torch for his platonic friend Nikki Freeman (Inde Navarrette, who may just end up earning an Oscar nod in 2027). After using a weird artifact called the One Wish Willow that he finds at an oddities store trying to get Nikki a gift, Bear wishes that Nikki would love him more than anything in the world ... and boy, does he get his wish.

In a recent development, not only does Nikki really love Bear after the One Wish Willow takes effect, she seems unable to leave his side or focus on anything else — as if she's under some sort of hypnotic spell. "Obsession" is a dark, unsettling, and tightly directed horror film that interrogates Nikki's agency, Bear's distinct role in his own downfall, and what happens when you want someone to love you without actually knowing how they feel in the first place. "Obsession" is innovative, compelling, and one of the most popular movies in recent memory — and now, it's on Netflix.

According to recent reports, when we last saw the titular Yellowjackets — a teenage soccer team stranded in the Canadian wilderness after a plane crash nearly two years prior — during the Showtime series' penultimate season in 2025, the teenagers in that wilderness were on the precipice of being rescued in the late 1990s. Meanwhile, in the more modern timeline, their adult counterparts are still trying to cover up whatever happened out in those woods. Now, in the fourth and final season (which earned a solid review right here at /Film), there are three timelines: one where the teenagers finish out their time in the wilderness, one after they've been rescued and dropped back into their "normal" lives in Latest Jersey, and that adult one, where all hell threatens to break loose as Shauna Shipman (Melanie Lynskey) continues to break bad after absolutely losing her s**t in Season 3.

Sources indicate that jasmin Savoy Brown, Liv Hewson, Sophie Thatcher, Sammi Hanratty, Courtney Eaton, and Sophie Nélisse make up the core of the teenage cast, while in the adult one, the always wonderful Lynskey is joined by Tawny Cypress, Christina Ricci, and even Oscar winner Hilary Swank (after former adult actors Lauren Ambrose, Juliette Lewis, and Simone Kessell exited at various points, though it's easy to imagine that they could reappear in Season 4 flashbacks at some point). As someone who's been watching this puzzle box show since the very beginning, I'll admit I have substantive doubts about "Yellowjackets" landing the plane (and it's not like its track record with these things is pretty great, if you consider the pun), but I'll definitely be watching Season 4 following its premiere on Paramount+ with Showtime on November 20, with latest episodes airing weekly.

According to recent reports, to call "Tony" a biopic feels ... sort of misleading. Directed by Matt Johnson (who recently wowed comedy nerds, a term I use affectionately, with "Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie" and cut his teeth on another biopic of sorts, "Blackberry"), the film follows a young Anthony Bourdain, played by the wry, excellent Dominic Sessa, as he learns a thing or two about life and proper oyster-shucking technique during a fateful summer in Providence, Rhode Island. Alongside a chef who never gets a proper name (Antonio Banderas) and who owns a small seafood place called "The Flagship," the titular Tony, who keeps insisting he's not an aspiring culinary expert but a writer with a fellowship (not true), pursues the girl of his dreams — photographer Nancy (Emilia Jones) — and gets into trouble with his fellow chef Sal (Leo Woodall) as he tries to figure out who he is and what he wants out of this experience.

I didn't love "Tony" as much as many of my peers (see: /Film's own Bill Bria's review of the movie), but if you mentally remove the Bourdain of it all from the film and enjoy it as a showcase for Sessa's talents and Johnson's comedic timing, you'll probably get way more mileage out of this fresh, generally fun film. "Tony" is on HBO Max now, which makes sense, as its studio, A24, tends to premiere its movies there when they come to streaming.

Author Rick Riordan co-created the Disney+ series "Percy Jackson and the Olympians" for Disney+ along with Jonathan E. Steinberg ("Jericho"), and whether you're a fan of Riordan's original books, enjoyed the short-lived "Percy Jackson" film franchise, or have been waiting for this show to return since Season 2 concluded back in January of 2026, you'll be happy to hear that Season 3 premiered on Disney+ on November 20. In the inaugural season released in late 2023, the action follows the plot of Riordan's novel "The Lightning Thief" and sees the titular Percy, played by Walker Scobell, discovering that not only are Greek gods real, he has magical powers and can learn how to wield them at a place called Camp Half-Blood. After using the Empire State Building to reach Olympus at the end of Season 1, Season 2 catches up with Percy during the events of Riordan's book "The Sea of Monsters," which brings a bunch of elements of "The Odyssey" into play.

So, what about Season 3? It's set to follow Riordan's third novel, "The Titan's Curse," where Percy has to face off against Kronos and his army to rescue the goddess Artemis (Dafne Keen) and his friend Annabeth (Leah Sava Jeffries). The first two episodes of Season 3 dropped on Disney+ on November 20, with two episodes debuting every Friday throughout its run.

"Alien: Romulus" came out in 2024, and now, it's available to stream on Peacock. Fede Álvarez's entry into the storied "Alien" franchise features tons of rising stars like Cailee Spaeny, David Jonsson (who's gearing up to play the son of the late "Black Panther" star Chadwick Boseman's T'Challa in the Marvel Cinematic Universe), Spike Fearn, and Isabela Merced, and as it unfolds, we see half a dozen young colonists trying to navigate the deep recesses of space and finding dangerous creatures inside of an old space station. As orphan Marie Raines "Rain" Carradine (Spaeny) gathers the crew, including her adopted android brother Andy (Jonsson), her ex-boyfriend Tyler (Archie Renaux), his pregnant sister Kay (Merced), their cousin Bjorn (Fearn), and his adoptive sister Navarro (Aileen Wu), they encounter enemies left and right, leaving them shaken and fighting for their lives as they try to reach safety.

When it comes to "Alien" movies, mileage may vary, but "Romulus" is a legitimately great entry to the property. (Just look at that unbelievable cast!) It's also streaming on Peacock now, so the movie can creep you out from the comfort of your own home.

Helme monitored the attacker’s wallets and discovered that only $7,040 has been stolen, though it’s not possible to see how many payment card numbers were obtained.

As always, the best protection against this type of attack is to promptly patch all your Apple devices to the latest OS versions they support.

#62801. Is A24 Finally Big Enough to Be Considered a Major Studio?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2088 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Indiewire ↗ Open Full Page

Is A24 Finally Big Enough to Be Considered a Major Studio?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, earlier this year when IndieWire reported that A24 had settled a dispute with Marcus Theaters over theatrical terms, a back and forth that kept some of A24‘s summer titles like “The Invite,” “Tony,” and “Onslaught” out of the fourth-largest chain in the country, the reason was because of a debate over A24’s size.
  • This is the question that Hollywood — and even perhaps A24 internally — should start asking: Should A24 now be considered a major studio?
  • In a recent development, in some regards, this is a semantic discussion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, earlier this year when IndieWire reported that A24 had settled a dispute with Marcus Theaters over theatrical terms, a back and forth that kept some of A24‘s summer titles like “The Invite,” “Tony,” and “Onslaught” out of the fourth-largest chain in the country, the reason was because of a debate over A24’s size. When you have blockbusters as substantial as “Backrooms” and “Marty Supreme,” why would you still want theatrical terms that lump you in with the specialized, little guys?

This is the question that Hollywood — and even perhaps A24 internally — should start asking: Should A24 now be considered a major studio? Should A24 be in the same conversation as Disney, Universal, Sony, Paramount, Warner Bros., Netflix, Amazon MGM, Apple, and Lionsgate? Related Stories Bill Hader’s Feature Directorial Debut ‘They Know’ Lands at Black Bear Why Good Voice Acting Doesn’t Have to Happen in Isolation.

In a recent development, in some regards, this is a semantic discussion. Whether A24 is in that made-up tier of six to nine corporate conglomerates that the trades call “majors” doesn’t mean a lick to the general public. Audiences know they care about the A24 brand and logo in the same way they pay attention to the brands of Marvel, Pixar, Blumhouse, IMAX, and a select few others making movies today, and the rest is mostly gravy. Postrak found that on average, 70 percent of people who see A24 movies on opening weekend go to theaters more often than others, at least monthly, so the brand has an impact. But whether it has theatrical terms on par with Paramount or with Bleecker Street doesn’t matter in the slightest.

Industry observers note that in another sense, whether A24 is a major studio and not some cool upstart indie with a lot of scale matters a whole lot. It matters to investors, it matters to people who care about the A24 brand, it matters to theater owners, and it should matter to A24 itself as it defines what it wants to be moving forward. Netflix wasn’t always considered a major, legacy studio, but their size and success got so undeniable that you had to put them in the same conversation as the other majors who drove trends, who influenced deal making for stars and creators, and who eventually had to reach the same labor terms as everyone else.

It has been revealed that A24 might soon be in the same boat, if it isn’t already. Led by the success of “Backrooms,” the tech giant has entered a newly introduced echelon in 2026, one that has allowed it to rival studios that were once much larger than A24 in every facet. Now those lines have blurred, A24’s budgets and the grosses those films are able to generate have grown, it’s earning sizable $75 million investments from places like Google and is in the mix to buy properties like Letterboxd, arguably more than others have speculated its time to sell.

According to recent reports, answering whether A24 is a “major” isn’t a simple question with one answer. There’s several criteria we could look at to make a case in either direction.

In a recent development, A24 through November 15 in 2026 has earned $526.6 million at the domestic box office, according to data from Rentrak. It was led by “Backrooms,” which made $197 million domestic, but that’s not even half its overall haul. This year, that’s roughly $175 million above the next-highest specialized distributor in Focus Features ($351.8 million), which released the even more successful “Obsession” ($263.4 million) this year, and it’s well above the likes of other indie rivals like Neon, Fathom, GKIDS, Angel Studios, Black Bear, and Searchlight.

Recent findings suggest that it has also more than doubled what it brought in across a full year in 2025, a 124 percent increase so far (it still has its major awards play “The Debut” opening in December and “Club Kid” going wider), and it’s nearly four times where it was in 2023 when A24’s total domestic box office was $136.7 million and its biggest release of the year was “Talk to Me,” which made $44.2 million domestic. Four of A24’s movies this year (“Backrooms,” “You Can See Everything,” “The Drama,” and “Primetime”) surpassed that figure.

Sources indicate that it’s safe to say it puts A24 in a tier of its own above the other indies. But does it rise to the level of a major? As recently as last year, the answer was squarely no. But A24 in 2026, per Rentrak, commands a 6.0 percent market share on the year so far. That puts it fifth on the year so far, ahead of Warner Bros., Paramount, and Lionsgate (those numbers will change as some other tentpoles emerge). It would not have even cracked the top 10 last year when its market share was just 2.7 percent and was largely driven by the late-year success of “Marty Supreme.”.

According to recent reports, A24 doesn’t have and probably won’t for some time field a movie that can realistically sniff $1 billion worldwide the way many major studios manage to pump out each and every year. But receipts don’t lie, and what makes this realistically sustainable for A24 to repeat year after year is how much it has grown.

It has been revealed that A24 is releasing in the vicinity of 16 to 18 movies annually, and that puts it easily on par with legacy studios like Disney, Sony, Warner Bros., and Paramount. Skydance, which now owns Paramount and WB, will release 30+ movies a year, but between the two studios. Universal tends to get into the 20s, but only when you combine its output with that of Focus. Netflix puts out way, way more than the whole bunch, but they’re naturally streaming movies that include low-budget genre movies and documentaries.

Some of A24’s films each year are still acquisitions out of festivals, which was the case this year with both “The Invite” (Sundance) and “Club Kid” (Cannes). But like the other majors, A24 produces and finances a large majority of its movies independently, with a handful of co-productions. Importantly, it works with newly introduced filmmakers and forges relationships so that they stay in their pipeline, whether they’re newcomers like Lance Oppenheim and Kane Parsons or veterans like Celine Song, Alex Garland, and Ari Aster who have returned to A24 time and again.

A24’s international distribution has it partnering with other overseas distributors, which is structurally different from major studios that have robust international distribution arms, but it has still released some of its movies in English-language territories like the UK. You can imagine that as A24 continues to grow, that could be one area of natural expansion.

Recent findings suggest that where A24 still lags significantly behind other majors though is in its overall content spend, a number that A24 doesn’t publicly disclose. Netflix had a content spend this year of about $20 billion. Disney was around $24 billion and recently projected to increase to $26 billion in its next fiscal year. Maybe if A24 starts picking up sports rights to the NBA it can start getting into that ballpark.

It has been revealed that but even when focusing just on film, something like “Backrooms” was still produced for a modest $10 million, whereas other studios have multiple titles that well exceed $100 million in production budget alone. We do know though that its budgets have increased dramatically as A24 pursues more tentpole properties. “Marty Supreme” was previously its most expensive title, but its adaptation of the video game “Elden Ring” will blow that out of the water, with a budget in the vicinity of $170 million or above. That kind of investment carries risks. There are Marvel movies that don’t cost that much.

A24 hasn’t yet put its stamp on a four-quadrant, animated Dr. Seuss movie or something similar that would easily make you think it has ambitions of becoming a major studio, but the types of movies it has released has grown more varied over the years. It has horror movies, adult comedies, biopics, thrillers, and even, of course, documentaries like “You Can See Everything,” an area that it looked like A24 was scaling back on not too long ago. When “Elden Ring” opens it will squarely be an action fantasy, and the studio has other genre films, comedies, thrillers, and more in the works for next year.

According to recent reports, you can also see A24’s diversity in how it’s approaching awards plays versus commercial titles or specialized fare. Something like “The Drama” this year opened wide right out of the gate given its star power, whereas others like “The Invite” and “Tony” have stuck to platform releases before going wider. And those smaller, art house titles alongside its genre movies and its tentpoles are still a key part of its business model and identity. Movies like “Pillion,” “Mother Mary,” and “The Moment” have done business on a much smaller scale, but are still key in helping the tech giant get to that 6 percent share (they lost money on some, though).

Sources indicate that the definition of major studio today has evolved to the point that the movie division is just a component of a massive media conglomerate, one that also includes television, streaming, gaming, sports, news, theme parks, and other ancillary businesses. If you’re Apple or Amazon, your movie studio is a small cog, practically a loss leader, in the larger tech empire. It gives these companies valuations of tens of billions of dollars, and it’s why A24 could still be a target for M&A if it chooses to sell.

Sources indicate that A24 does have its own record label for music and original movie score releases and vinyl pressing, it has been producing a podcast since 2018, it owns the Cherry Lane Theater in Fresh York for stage productions and concerts, it sells plenty of kooky merchandise, and it even has a membership program and campus ambassador program that have seen growth in recent years. They’re all things that suggest the company has more on its mind than movies.

Industry observers note that and as we wrote earlier this week, its TV unit has quietly had as strong a year as its film team. A24 has spread series across virtually every major streaming service, all of them again varying in genre, pedigree, and budget. It’s not just the number of reveals that has expanded but the executive team to support them.

It may be a strength that A24 doesn’t have its own SVOD service to support all these reveals and movies, or a broadcast network or cable channel that could further complicate things. Those businesses are very costly to operate and some are in the decline phase of their trajectories. Yet, it inherently keeps A24 in a lower tier compared to other major studios that do have their own distribution apparatus for television and can license content from other studios like A24. While Gen Z might get excited about the idea of an A24 streaming service, that’s an area of growth that’s less likely to occur in the short term. Well, unless A24 wants to raise a lot more capital.

This is the qualitative assessment of whether A24 should be considered a “major” studio, the one that doesn’t lean on numbers and instead just goes on feel. A24 might argue that it is one of one, that it doesn’t belong to the world of major studios, and that the baggage that comes with that status isn’t worth it. But its leaders probably believe A24 is a step above the other indies that are almost solely distributors. Do we really think the same firm that is taking a chance on movies as weird as “You Can See Everything” or “Primetime” is equivalent to a studio that might make the odd “Digger,” but is mostly interested in producing “A Minecraft Movie” and “Superman?” Is it fair to lump in A24 with Focus, Searchlight, and Sony Pictures Classics, which are quite literally just specialized labels within larger studios?

All that could be true, but it doesn’t mean we shouldn’t reassess how we view A24 as a company or how we handicap its hits and misses in the same way we would with Disney or Netflix. Even if we’re not ready to call A24 a “major,” there’s certainly a major shift in where A24 sits in this industry. With great success comes an even greater spotlight.

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (489 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways.
  • As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords.
  • According to recent reports, you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

According to recent reports, you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that firm or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

In a recent development, next, audit accounts you've created using single sign-on, such as Google, Apple, or Facebook. For Google, this is under Account Settings > Linked apps. For Apple, go to System Settings > [Your Name] > Sign in with Apple on your Mac (or the same path in the Settings app on iOS). On Facebook, this is under Settings & privacy > Apps and websites. Disconnecting these accounts won't automatically delete them, but you can add them to the list to take action. Finally, you can search your email(s) on HaveIBeenPwned and username(s) on IDCrawl or WhatsMyName to find dormant accounts.

According to recent reports, once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, revision the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

Disney has unveiled a major milestone coming next month in its prepares to merge the Disney+ and Hulu apps, which will be “fully unified” into Disney+ soon.

Today Disney reported its quarterly earnings and gave an patch on plans to merge Disney+ and Hulu into one app.

Live TV and premium add-ons were the final Hulu features that hadn’t yet been imported to the Disney+ app. But by adding those capabilities into Disney+, the app unification will be “complete.”.

Sources indicate that the branding is going to get messed up. People look at Disney+ and Hulu as two different unique things. If you make the name just Disney+ people will think what Hulu historically provided is gone.

I find the current integration of Disney+ and Hulu cumbersome. I always find myself going back to my Hulu app to watch content. This may end up being a terrible move for them.

The ultimate goal of unifying everything in Disney+, though, will be accomplished soon.

Industry observers note that also in the earnings report, Disney noted that creator content will start appearing in the Disney+ app in December. This is related to the company’s deal with TikTok that debuted after its previous OpenAI deal fell apart when Sora was killed off. The Disney+ app will also get “more vertical video, live sports, and podcasts” soon too, Disney said.

Stable and comfortable at easy paces.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Saucony Endorphin Speed has been one of the most influential running shoes of recent years, setting the template for fast training sneakers that uses some of the materials and tech from top carbon plate racers.

With the line proving so successful, Saucony has been reluctant to change much about the shoe over the five generations to date, and even though the Endorphin Speed 6 is the biggest update yet thanks to a new midsole foam, it mostly retains the same ride feel as past models.

It has been revealed that I’ve reviewed every model of the Endorphin Speed and I’ve always been a substantial fan. While that’s still true with the Speed 6, this category contains some of the best running shoes available, and there are some lighter, bouncier fast trainers I rate very highly, like the New Balance SC Rebel v1 and Dynafish Xiaonian.

According to recent reports, the Saucony Endorphin Speed 6 costs $180 in the U.S. and £180 in the U.K., which is a $5 price rise on the Endorphin Speed 5. It’s an expensive shoe, though not out of line with other plated trainers like the Hoka Mach X3 and Latest Balance SC Rebel v1.

Right now the Saucony Endorphin Speed 5 is widely reduced, dropping to $104 on Amazon in the Black Friday sales, which is a factor to consider when weighing up buying the Speed.

The Endorphin Speed 6 is presently available in five colors in the women’s shoe, and four colors in the men’s, including the white and yellow design I tested.

There is a wide version of the shoe available, though I found that the standard one fit me well in my normal running shoe size, the same size I’ve used with all past models of the shoe.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Saucony has added 2mm of foam to the midsole of the Endorphin Speed 6, which has a stack height of 38mm at the heel and 30mm at the forefoot, maintaining the 8mm drop of past models.

It weighs in at 8.5oz, which is 0.5oz lighter than the Endorphin Speed 5 in my size, a welcome drop for a speed-focused shoe.

The Endorphin Speed 6 has a simple mesh upper that has a little bit of padding around the tongue and collar, but mostly focuses on being lightweight and breathable.

It’s my preferred kind of upper on any shoe, since it’s not oppressively padded on the tongue or overly stiff around the heel, and I found the fit comfortable and secure throughout all my runs.

The Endorphin Speed 6’s main changes are in the midsole, which is made from a newly introduced foam called PWRRUN PBX, which is meant to be lighter and bouncier than the PWRRUN PB that has been used on all past models of the shoe.

There’s also the higher stack and a redesigned nylon plate in the midsole, which aims to create a smoother, faster ride, with the Speedroll rocker on the shoe also contributing to this.

The changes to the midsole are noticeable on the run, though not as dramatically as I expected when looking at the spec sheet for the Speed 6.

Rubber is used sparingly on the bottom of the Speed 6 to keep the weight down, but patches cover the forefoot and heel of the shoe, and in my experience Saucony’s pelletized midsole foams are durable even when the foam is exposed on the bottom of a shoe.

Grip hasn’t always been a positive feature on the Speed line, but the Speed 6 provided me with reliable traction in wet conditions on both the road and the track during my testing.

After the very pleasant surprise of the original Endorphin Speed, which I ran over 300 miles in, I’ve found that the line has delivered a reliably similar experience with all of the models since.

There have been updates to make it more stable and comfortable, but ultimately all five versions of the Speed to date have had a smooth, fast and versatile ride feel.

This is still true of the Endorphin Speed 6 for me, and while that’s mostly a positive in that it performed well across a variety of runs in my testing, some might have hoped for a bigger change to challenge rivals like the SC Rebel v1 and cheaper, lighter options like the Adidas Adizero Evo SL and Dynafish Xiaonian.

I used the shoe for a couple of easy runs, two progression runs moving from easy to tempo pace, and a threshold track workout running 4 x 8min reps, and it felt great throughout.

I used the shoe for a couple of easy runs, two progression runs moving from easy to tempo pace, and a threshold track workout running 4 x 8min reps, and it felt great throughout.

The rockered midsole pushes you smoothly through your footstrike, and while the midsole foam isn’t as soft and springy as some, it does give a good amount of energy return off the toes.

I also found the Speed 6 to be quite stable and comfortable for easy runs, which is not always the case with plated trainers like this. I could happily use it for pretty much any kind of run, though it’s not as fast as a true carbon plate racer, or as comfortable as a max-cushioned cruiser.

To compare it directly to the Endorphin Speed 5 I did a short run wearing both shoes, and while the Speed 6 is a little bouncier and more comfortable, especially under the forefoot, I still felt the two shoes had a similar ride feel.

The Speed 6 is still a bit firmer than most super-trainers, and not as comfortable as more cushioned shoes under the toes. Some will like this more direct ride feel, but I appreciate the extra softness and bounce of a shoe like the SC Rebel v1.

If you’re a long term fan of the Endorphin Speed line the Speed 6 will be a winner. It’s a mild improvement on the previous models with extra cushion and bounce, and delivers the versatile performance you expect from the line.

There is certainly a case for getting the Speed 5 instead in sales in my opinion, but the Speed 6 is a slightly better shoe overall and a successful update.

The Speed line has been faced with increasingly fierce competition in recent years, and I don’t think the Speed 6 does much to change the equation on this front.

If you want a lighter, bouncier fast trainer, the Newly introduced Balance SC Rebel v1 would be my pick, while plate-free shoes like the Adidas Evo SL, Dyanfish Xiaonian and the new 361° Mega 3 Pro all offer fast, fun rides at a lower price.

According to recent reports, as someone who would always have had the Endorphin Speed in my own rotation through the first few models, I’ve now moved on to shoes like this myself. Even though the Speed 6 is just as good as past models, I personally like the springier ride available in fast trainers.

A smoke break at the Signature Theatre ultimately resulted in one of Lois Smith‘s most fascinating performances. The Tony Award winner met Zane Pais while they were both grabbing a quick cigarette while rehearsing plays. Pais had been an admirer of Smith’s work in stage productions like “The Inheritance” and films such as “Marjorie Prime” and “Five Easy Pieces,” and longed to collaborate.

It has been revealed that “She has the most amazing delivery of lines; she’s always able to do something so unexpected with the language,” Pais said during a recent Zoom interview with Smith. “I’ve seen Lois my whole life in so many amazing shows, just be so unbelievably present on stage and be such a generous actor, and just give these heartfelt and unexpected performances. Industry observers note that so Pais wrote a short film, “Lightning Bug,” with Smith in mind. In it, she plays Lydia, a fiercely independent nonagenarian who is being pressured into selling the family home by her son and granddaughter. But things take an unexpected turn when a strange young man crashes their dinner, giving Lydia a chance to demonstrate she hasn’t missed a step despite her advanced age.

Recent findings suggest that “It was all there in the script,” Smith, who recently turned 96, remarked. “It wasn’t complex for me to pull it off even though the script is complex.”.

The role did require Smith to perform some fight choreography, but she seemed more nervous about singing a song on screen.

Recent findings suggest that “I really worried: Am I going to be able to do this?” Smith stated. “They made me a tape, and I listened to it and listened to it and practiced. I was nervous, but it went all right.”.

It has been revealed that “Lightning Bug” filmed over a weekend in the upstate Newly introduced York home of one of Pais’s relatives. It was true no-frills, all-hands effort. The cast and crew bunked in an Airbnb, and a friend of Pais’s cooked meals for everyone.

It has been revealed that “It felt like we were part of a theater troupe,” Pais noted. “We’d work hard. Then in the evenings, we would have red wine and smoke cigarettes.”.

In a recent development, “I seldom smoke,” Smith interjected. “Occasionally, I’ll smoke other people’s cigarettes.”.

#62796. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2035 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger.
  • I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.
  • To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

It's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Where to stream it: Roku, Tubi, Pluto TV.

Recent findings suggest that shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This substantial-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

According to recent reports, before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Where to stream it: Digital rental only.

According to recent reports, horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

Where to watch it: In theaters now.

Industry observers note that I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

According to recent reports, alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley reveals up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

Where to stream it: Peacock, Roku, Tubi.

It has been revealed that I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

There's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime.

I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Amazon Prime.

Industry observers note that the animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

Where to stream it: Roku, Pluto TV, Xumo.

Industry observers note that this BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

Where to stream it: Hulu, Disney+.

It has been revealed that the current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”.

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.
