📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

Recent findings suggest that you can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Industry observers note that would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.).

According to recent reports, in the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Industry observers note that here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart promptly led to women posting the waist heart.

Sources indicate that okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

Recent findings suggest that as if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?".

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood.".

Recent findings suggest that nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

A few years ago, Bay returned to blockbuster filmmaking with Ambulance, the action thriller starring Jake Gyllenhaal (The Day After Tomorrow) and Yahya Abdul-Mateen II (Wonder Man). The 2022 film grossed just over $50 million at the box office against a $40 million budget, and it’s now streaming on Netflix for those who missed out on seeing it on the major screen. Bay was briefly attached to direct the new Netflix action thriller Fast and Loose, starring Will Smith, but he backed out of the film due to creative differences that arose between him and the leading star — the Bad Boys reunion will have to wait.

It has been revealed that the future is a bit murky for Bay right now, and while it’s been reported that he’s returning to the Transformers franchise to direct a upcoming film, practically nothing is known about the project at this time. Many fans would like to see Bay get back to the same schedule he had in the early to mid 2010s when he was directing films at least every other year. One of Bay’s most polarizing and entertaining movies came back in 2016 when he teamed up with John Krasinski (The Office) for 13 Hours, which is based on Mitchell Zuckoff’s book of the same name. It tells the story of the six U.S. operatives stationed at an off-the-books CIA base in Benghazi who are called into action when the compound falls under attack by a horde of armed locals.

13 Hours, formerly titled 13 Hours: The Secret Soldiers of Benghazi, is streaming on Paramount+ in America, and the film has even surged into the top 10 in the last few days and is one of the most-watched titles on the platform. For those without a Paramount+ subscription, the film is also available to watch on Peacock, and it’s even streaming for free via Pluto TV. Additional cast members for the film include Pablo Schreiber as Kris Paronto, James Badge Dale as Tyrone Woods, and David Denmam as Dave Benton. The film is a must-watch for fans of other classic war thrillers like Black Hawk Down and Zero Dark Thirty.

Check out 13 Hours on Paramount+ or Peacock and stay tuned to Collider for more updates and coverage of Michael Bay’s past and future projects.

  • In a recent development, however, South Park’s constant controversies can sometimes come at a cost to the series.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Although South Park season 29’s Rotten Tomatoes audience rating might seem surprisingly low at first glance, the show’s most recent response actually makes a lot of sense when considered in the broader context of its history. While The Simpsons has been on the air for longer than South Park and has many more episodes to its name than the Comedy Central hit, no one could deny that South Park is definitely the more controversial of the two highlights.

Industry observers note that admittedly, The Simpsons has the controversial character Apu, and a handful of episodes from the ‘90s and 2000s that have aged badly. However, South Park is one of TV’s most controversial shows ever, and the series has remained jaw-dropping in its commitment to boundary-pushing content even after almost three decades on the air. There is probably no other show on TV that could get away with depicting the current US President’s sentient penis flying off his body as he uses the toilet.

In a recent development, however, South Park’s constant controversies can sometimes come at a cost to the series. Fans of the anarchic animated comedy might be surprised to find out that, although most online reviewers of season 29 have been largely positive on an episode-by-episode basis, South Park season 29’s current Rotten Tomatoes audience rating sits at a shockingly low 44%. However, this doesn’t really come as a surprise, and it shouldn’t necessarily worry viewers, given the show’s history.

Longtime South Park viewers will recall that the show has always endured mixed reviews since its 1997 premiere, when plenty of critics called season 1 crass, unpleasant, and un-funny. Since then, some of South Park’s most controversial episodes have undoubtedly caused outrage, but plenty of the show’s more straightforwardly divisive episodes have also simply been written off as purely annoying by fans and critics alike.

Ironically, for a show that’s constantly reinventing itself, South Park viewers and critics historically hate changes to the show’s status quo. The responses to season 4, episode 14, “Pip,” epitomized this concern, as many fans were furious about South Park’s decision to forget about Cartman, Stan, Kyle, and Kenny for a week as the show instead opted to parody Charles Dickens' legendary Bildungsroman Great Expectations. The fact that “Pip” was funny and inventive didn’t factor into frustration with its divergence from South Park’s status quo.

Similarly, season 2’s premiere, “Terrance and Phillip in Not Without My Anus,” was South Park’s most widely hated episode for years since the episode also ignored the show’s main characters. Admittedly, season 1’s cliffhanger ending meant this outing was a straightforward example of South Park’s creators intentionally trolling its fans, but the outsized opprobrium that met the prank highlights the same recurring issue.

Sources indicate that much like South Park making Randy a main character was a divisive fan base-splitting maneuver for years, most of the show’s divergences from its status quo have been with frustration. Even season 17’s serialized three-part ending earned the season a Rotten Tomatoes rating of only 60%, further proving that South Park viewers seemingly don’t take kindly to change.

While an audience rating of 44% might sound fairly brutal, it is worth putting this number in context. South Park season 28’s audience rating is a mere 31%, even though its finale was a hilarious, transgressive Christmas special that managed to tie together a flurry of absurd, utterly disconnected storylines. Meanwhile, the biggest new TV show of 2026, CBS’s SEAL Team replacement Marshals, currently has an audience rating of only 28%.

Sources indicate that within this context, the news that South Park has been hit with mixed reviews hardly seems so out of the ordinary or worrying for the show’s future. That mentioned, it is amusing to see just how much South Park’s audience capture may have worked against the show’s reception. South Park has repeatedly been criticized for typically condemning any major divergence from the social and cultural status quo, so it is perhaps unsurprising that the show has found fans who don’t appreciate change.

According to recent reports, for years, most of South Park’s biggest mistakes, from the transphobia of season 23, episode 7, “Board Girls,” to the climate change denial of the original ManBearPig storyline, have been rooted in a defense of the status quo. As such, South Park’s poor critical reception could reasonably be attributed to a pro-status quo show making experimental episodes that intentionally mess with the show’s own status quo.

According to recent reports, that being said, South Park season 29’s story also offers another reason for its mixed reception. South Park is a gleefully offensive series, and one that doesn’t pull its punches when aiming at every target under the sun. Inevitably, a vocal portion of South Park’s fan base would eventually become upset with season 29’s brutal skewering of billionaires and Trump, and voice this anger online.

Recent findings suggest that south Park is and always has been, since the original inception of the series, a dark, transgressive political satire, so the show really shouldn’t be earning universally positive audience feedback across the board. The same viewers who might have cheered on episodes like “Board Girls” may well hate to see Trump ruthlessly lampooned in “Billionaire Weenietown,” and vice versa. Like any politically charged series, South Park should ultimately be ruffling the feathers of its viewers at times.

It has been revealed that ironically, it might South Park season 29’s willingness to address controversial topics that makes this outing so divisive. South Park has always claimed to be a series that is willing to take on any event or subject, no matter how taboo, but the show has also been known to lapse into laziness at times when meeting a tight deadline or struggling to find news stories of note to explore.

As such, there were always guaranteed to be some fans of South Park who only appreciated the show’s satire when it was aimed at subjects they disliked, and this could account for the show’s divided critical reception in season 29. In any case, the reality is that South Park isn’t going anywhere any time soon, no matter how much its Rotten Tomatoes rating might decline in the meantime.

Disney now seems to have warmed to the idea like a cup of hot cocoa, especially thanks to the two additional names who are working with Culkin on the project: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg. Related Stories What ‘Digger’ Has in Common with Gary Oldman’s Winston Churchill and Charlize Theron’s Megyn Kelly ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Review: PTA’s Spellbinding Concert Doc Is a Gorgeously Tender Performance.

Disney’s 20th Century Studios is in early development on a sequel to “Home Alone” that would star Culkin reprising his original role and in which Rogen and Goldberg on behalf of their Point Grey banner would write and produce the film, working with Culkin on his idea, IndieWire has learned.

Things are very, very early days, and any plot details are being kept under wraps for now, and no director is attached at the moment.

Sources indicate that chris Columbus directed the original “Home Alone” and its nearly-as-loved sequel “Home Alone 2: Lost in New York,” and both written by the late great John Hughes. If you can believe it, there have been six “Home Alone” movies in all, with the third one at least released in theaters and doing respectable box office numbers. The others are all TV movies or in the case of the most recent 2021 film “Home Sweet Home Alone,” a Disney+ streaming movie.

Industry observers note that the original two films though grossed $477 million and $358 million worldwide, respectively, and the original still gets tons of cable play and finds its way into the Nielsen streaming charts. It makes sense that a more serious sequel with Culkin back in the fold would be welcomed by audiences.

Sadly, “Home Alone” has been back on the minds of audiences of late after the recent passing of Catherine O’Hara, who played Kevin’s mom, and also Tim Curry, who had a small role as a hotel clerk in “Home Alone 2.” Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern as the Wet Bandits are still around, though Pesci has been mostly retired outside of his return in Scorsese’s “The Irishman” back in 2019 and his role in the Pete Davidson Peacock series “Bupkis” in 2023.

Culkin too has had a bit of a resurgence, making a cameo in the most recent season of “Fallout” and doing a voice in Disney’s “Zootopia 2.”.

Google Wallet is now available on iOS to “organize purchases, tickets, boarding passes, and more in one easy place” in the US.

The Google Wallet app on iPhone does not offer tap-to-pay functionality due to platform restrictions. Instead, Google touts three intended use cases:.

Sources indicate that app navigation is handled by a floating pill (in Liquid Glass) with two tabs. The homepage starts with a carousel of recent purchases slated for delivery, followed by boarding passes, and finally a grid of loyalty cards.

The next tab highlights a list of recent transactions associated with Google. The Wallet app will display purchase emails and summarize them. You also get a list of Passes, which you can pin/unpin from the homepage, and payment methods saved to your Google Account.

The ‘plus’ FAB (floating action button) lets you add loyalty, gift, and payment cards (for use in Chrome). There’s a convenient “Everything else” camera scanner that can be used to digitize anything else.

The other main reason Google Wallet now exists on iOS is that the company wants the app to be a “secure hub for managing agentic purchases across Google.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • That’s why I drove the Hyundai Ioniq 9 Calligraphy Design for the second time this year — just to convince myself that there are better 3-row midsize SUVs out there.
  • But after another week behind the wheel, I can tell you firsthand that judging the Ioniq 9 by its cover is a mistake.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that quite frankly, the Hyundai Ioniq 9 gets a bad rap for the way it looks. In fact, I stated in my 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 9 review that the design is an “odd mashup featuring a curvy front bumper with an even stranger-looking arched rear.” It’s one of the last SUVs I’d expect to win any beauty awards.

That’s why I drove the Hyundai Ioniq 9 Calligraphy Design for the second time this year — just to convince myself that there are better 3-row midsize SUVs out there. I’ve spent more time testing 3-row SUVs than any other vehicle type this year, with models like the Kia Telluride, Volvo XC90, Volkswagen Atlas, and Lucid Gravity getting my seal of approval.

But after another week behind the wheel, I can tell you firsthand that judging the Ioniq 9 by its cover is a mistake. Here’s what I realized.

Best long distance driving efficiency.

Best short distance driving efficiency.

As with most vehicles, fuel economy and efficiency tend to dwindle over time — which is why I’m shocked that the Ioniq 9 is an exception. I was already impressed by the 3 mi/kWh average I got when I drove it last year, yet my second run delivered even better results.

In a recent development, across 130.5 miles of mixed driving, my second go-around with the Ioniq 9 yielded an impressive 3.3 mi/kWh. What surprised me even more was the substantial improvement in city driving, where I recorded a peak tally of 4.5 mi/kWh — up from my previous best of 3.8 mi/kWh.

Considering it’s marketed as a three-row family hauler, it’s remarkable that the Ioniq 9 can post numbers like this. That extra efficiency is critical, too: while this trim carries an EPA-estimated range of 311 miles, averaging 3.3 mi/kWh puts its real-world range closer to 363 miles.

I’ll admit I was harsh on the Hyundai Ioniq 9’s styling the first time around. While it certainly takes cues from the subcompact Hyundai Kona, I argued that it was an odd mashup that was confused about what aesthetic it was trying to go after.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

It has been revealed that after spending another week with it, though, its unconventional look slowly grew on me — even if that appreciation is mostly isolated to the front of the EV. That’s due to Hyundai’s signature Parametric Pixel LED light bar, which stretches across the nose like something straight out of a sci-fi movie. Those individual blocks give it a retro look that becomes even more dazzling from dusk into the night. In a sea of generic crossovers, this one certainly commands road presence.

That remarked, I still haven’t come to terms with the back half of this electric SUV. That tapered, upright rear end remains the hardest pill to swallow, giving it the look of a boat tail. Despite this, I now appreciate that the shape is doing the heavy lifting to make it aerodynamic — and subsequently boosting its efficiency.

It has been revealed that whether I’m making a quick stop at the local grocery store or on my 30+ mile commute to work, the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 9 doesn’t skimp on the comforts. Step inside, and it’s clear Hyundai prioritized first-class comfort for the people riding up front and in the middle.

For example, the plush H-Tex seats strike a great balance of softness and support — which, for the driver, includes extra pampering courtesy of Hyundai’s Ergo Motion seat. When activated, it slowly adjusts the firmness of the cushion, sort of like getting a mini massage while driving, all to deter fatigue on longer hauls.

Still, the real VIP treatment belongs to the second-row captain’s chairs. With both heating and ventilation, plus power-reclining backrests and extendable footrests, they turn the middle row into a rolling lounge. However, the third row leaves more to be desired. Although I still appreciate having the extra seating capacity in a pinch, the legroom back there is practically nonexistent for adults — so I’d much rather keep that rear bench folded flat to make way for more trunk space.

At nearly $80,000 as tested, the Ioniq 9 Calligraphy Design comes loaded with just about every luxury and tech perk anyone could ask for — and rightfully so.

According to recent reports, ​I still absolutely love Hyundai's adaptive cruise control, which makes long drives bearable and includes a dedicated lane-centering button on the steering wheel that also happens to work on local roads. Adding to that is a crisp Head-Up Display that projects my speed and navigation right onto the windshield.

​Changing lanes is effortless thanks to the Blind-Spot View Monitor (which streams a live camera feed straight into the digital gauge cluster) and a digital rearview mirror that offers a wider field of view than a conventional glass mirror.

​Back-seat passengers get plenty of love, too, with built-in rear side-window sunshades, a massive panoramic sunroof, and dazzling customizable ambient lighting that sets an upscale mood after dark.

​There’s also practical utility in the form of a handy 120V outlet accessible right in the trunk, letting me power laptops, tailgating gear, or small appliances straight off the SUV’s battery.

At nearly $80,000 as tested, the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 9 Calligraphy Design is easily one of the most expensive vehicles in Hyundai’s entire lineup — and that price tag has long made me a skeptic.

​Yet spending a second week behind the wheel proved that judging it at face value is a mistake. Between its even better real-world efficiency, spacious cabin suited for families, and a laundry list of thoughtful luxury features, the Ioniq 9 delivers where it counts most: a family hauler that's rich in utility and backed by an efficient drive.

Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 measures whether changes to real codebases are good enough for maintainers to merge.

Tech Report: How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (939 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing.
  • “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire.
  • Recent findings suggest that the lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be important for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing. It happens at a goodbye party for Raissa Molina (Liza Soberano), who is heading to Caltech. Her best friend Jo (H.E.R.) is late to the party and asks around to see where Raissa is, when an older woman points with her lips in the right direction. It’s a small moment, a visual gag that can easily go over the audience’s heads amidst all the other jokes in the sequence. But audiences familiar with Filipino culture immediately caught on to it, as did Latino fans and many others who recognize that gesture as the most potent and accurate way to point at something. Related Stories ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’.

“That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire. “Growing up around Filipinos, the lip point was something that was so specific and unique to me, so it’s beautiful that it transcends into other cultures. Adding that felt like a celebration of it, but also something that makes characters feel real. And in adding that specificity about the culture, it ends up being the most universal aspect of the movie because it invites everyone in.”.

Recent findings suggest that the lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be important for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation. Later in the film, Jo does the lip pointing because an animator thought it would be a good idea to reprise it, after learning about its place in the culture. Indeed, in addition to having an authentically Filipino cast and a cultural consultant to really capture Filipino culture, the animation team found their own ways of homaging or capturing aspects of Filipino culture to bring to the movie.

When creating the character of Jo, the animation team based a lot of her hand expressions on Filipino skater Margie Didal and her own hand gestures, while the villainous Manananggal’s movements were created by the animation team watching choreography done by Filipino-American dancer Phil Tayag, who brought a pop locking influence to the vampire-like creature.

It has been revealed that “When we first approached DreamWorks and Universal with this story, it was important to everybody that we got every detail of this story and this culture right,” director Januel Mercado said. “.

After challenging what was thought possible with DreamWorks animated films in “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” Crawford and Mercado push the studio’s visuals forward with “Forgotten Island.” With most of the story taking place on the island of Nakali, which is populated by all sorts of mythical creatures, to really capture the fantastical possibilities of this world, the movie’s visuals go wild, taking inspiration from 1990s Filipino art as well as anime from that time period.

Industry observers note that for Crawford, the major lesson learned from “The Last Wish” was that you could take big swings in the animation style and the visuals, but you could also do specific things in the story with those visuals. Indeed, when it came to “Forgotten Island,” the idea of memories and friendship became not only central to the story of Jo and Raissa, but also to the eclectic visual styles represented in the movie.

Industry observers note that “The idea became that we could push the animation styles to represent the different ways people recall memories,” Crawford explained. “We didn’t need to be limited by Western CG-style animation, but actually bring in some of our own nostalgia into it and make sure it fit the characters. When Raww tries to explain what happened when he met Jo and Raissa, he sees himself as way cooler than he is, so he sees himself as Goku or Guile from ‘Street Fighter,’ the animation going 2D in an action-heavy tone. But when we meet Mermahn, he is very shallow and narcissistic, and we felt his glamorous point of view fit the aesthetic of ‘Sailor Moon’ with the silly kind of heart-shaped lens flare.”.

In a recent development, still, just because you can go Super Saiyan doesn’t mean you let go of reality. Instead, the directors worked with the head of cinematography, Scott Cullen, to make sure the film had a live-action look to it. The idea was to capture the nostalgia of growing up, while being able to feel the camera in the space the action takes place in, as if it was a physical set.

Industry observers note that “Joel and I really wanted to make sure you feel like live-action, you feel the cameras there, and the way the light interacts with the lens is reminiscent of tangible photos we grew up taking, where you don’t know how they’ll develop,” Mercado said. “ We wanted to add imperfections, and to have interaction of weather on the camera, like condensation of rain and droplets on the camera.”.

This all added to making “Forgotten Island” look like a part of the evolution of DreamWorks Animation, while standing out as something entirely fresh and unique. As Crawford mentioned, the studio doesn’t really have a specific house style like other significant studios. “Every movie requires innovation and pushing boundaries and finding solutions,” he added.

Froggatt also discusses Jan's mindset going into the finale and where she thinks she and Harry land before her untimely death. How early on in the season did you know that Jan would not be long for this world?

It's major drama, big stakes, high stakes; it's shocks, and the things you least expect are what you see on screen — so, it's always been there. And also, with Jan starting out as a character in Season 2, saying to Harry that she wants a divorce, it's kind of, like, where does that then lead them? She's either got to get on board and join the family business, which, why would she do that after 20-odd years? Or she's got to follow it through at some point. So one way or another, she was kind of destined to not be there for the whole thing. [Laughs].

I've had to do two seasons. I'm so thrilled because I've just had the most wonderful storylines, and it's been an amazing opportunity and journey. I've always wanted to do a gangster genre, so it was a real bucket list thing for me to do; I wanted to play a gangster or a gangster's wife, and I got to do that. I always wanted to work with Guy Ritchie, and this amazing creative team created by Ronan Bennett and Jez Butterworth's beautiful words. It's been an absolute ball.

Sources indicate that I feel like in the last few episodes, Jan was of already in this in-between world, because she just killed Donnie, she's still struggling to figure out what to do, and her and Harry are in this tenuous position. What do you think was going on in her head as she was lying in that bath in the penultimate episode?

Industry observers note that FROGGATT: Yeah, I think there's a lot going through her head, as always. I think, at that stage, Harry's told her, right, you're gonna get on a flight, and you and Gina can go somewhere hot, sunny, and he may or may not have promised that he's gonna come too? But if he did promise he was gonna come, he probably didn't mean for very long. So I think there's that. I think she's sort of contemplating her life, really. Like, what got her to this point? The decisions she's made, the things she's been dragged into. The fact that she's crossed this line, where she's taken her life, and she is changed forever because of that. There's still that yearning that she just wants some normality, you know? A normal family life, and she's never gonna have that.

Industry observers note that I think it's interesting because at the end of the season, right before everything happens, Harry seems like he's going on a vacation. You know, he tells Conrad, you can call me whenever, but I'm going somewhere with my family.

Industry observers note that FROGGATT: Yes, exactly. On a holiday, yeah, and they'll probably stay, and he'll come back and carry on. That's how I saw it, and then sadly, they never get to do that holiday together.

I'm curious, at that point, do you think Jan's still intent on divorcing Harry, or have things turned around for her a little bit? She's always going to be attached to Harry. Is there a part of her where she's like, well, he's trying to be a husband again, maybe we don't need to get divorced?

Sources indicate that FROGGATT: Yeah, I think in my mind, by this stage... I think after Jan and Harry have met, and Jan's told him that she's killed Donnie, and he already knows, and he's already cleaned up her "mess," I think there's a latest respect there, again, for each other. Even though they'd separated, she'd slept with someone else, and then she did this terrible thing, Harry was still the only person in the world, on the whole planet Earth, that she could be truly, truly honest with, and who would always have her back.

Recent findings suggest that so, I think that bond is reignited there. So I don't think Jan's necessarily looking for divorce, but they've reached this crossroads where something has to change, and I think that something is probably Jan and Gina disappearing off into the sunset. And Harry may be popping in every so often for a holiday. Who knows what that would have been? But, but they don't get the chance to find out, sadly.

There's a very interesting scene when Gina and Jan are at the safe house, and they're talking, and Gina tells her about the conversation that her and her dad had, and I think for Gina, she's like, "Oh, it's actually a really comforting conversation," but what's going on in Jan's mind at that moment? Because I would be worried, as a mom, like, "I didn't want you to end up with someone like Harry, but you might become Harry at this point.".

FROGGATT: Yeah, exactly. Well, it's not what any parent wants for their child, is it? And any loving parent wants their children to do better than they did. So they want them to make better choices than the choices they made, and you try and teach your children more than you knew at their age, and you try and give them more tools than you had, and the things you've learned, and it's the same for Jan. She doesn't want Gina to carry on in Jan's footsteps, but even less so, Harry's, probably. Well, I don't know, which is worse? Maybe it's worse to be Jan, actually.

FROGGATT: He's in control of it.

FROGGATT: At least he's gonna teach you to be in control, which is no bad thing.

According to recent reports, I think from Harry's point of view, he's also trying to do that. He's like, "Oh, I'll let you into this world; I'll be the guide for you." But I don't think that's what Jan expected her husband to say.

FROGGATT: I mean, whether she expected him to or not, I'm not sure, but it's certainly not what she wants him to say, definitely not.

Industry observers note that what do you think Jan's death will do for Gina and Harry moving forward? Should we as an audience be worried for or about them?

FROGGATT: Well, who knows? Time will tell. I know they've just started filming Season 3, because I've been in touch with some of the guys, so I'm excited to see what the aftermath is of Jan's death, but obviously Gina's going to be devastated, because that's her mum, you know? That's going to have a huge fallout for Gina and Harry. At the end of the day, Jan was still Harry's best friend, really, despite all their difficulties and ups and downs, and all the difficulties that they've been through in Season 2. They could still be honest with each other and still rely on each other to keep each other's faith. So, Harry has lost that.

Recent findings suggest that no matter where their relationship was romantically, he's still lost his partner in life. So, Harry being Harry will probably — as Frankie does in Season 2 — not want to be taken off task. Harry being Harry will probably, you know, not let emotions rule him, I imagine, but, at the same time, yeah, it'll be interesting to see how it all unfolds.

Before I let you go, I love Tim Kring, and I'm very curious about the latest Magnificent Seven show. I want to know if you could give us any updates on that, because I'm really looking forward to it.

In a recent development, FROGGATT: It's really exciting. Yeah, it was so much fun to film. We finished at the end of September, so we did four months in Alberta, and it was a wonderful experience. I've just seen a few little clips when I've been in to do ADR, redoing the sound, and it looks incredible. It looks so exciting, and it's like adventure and drama, and it's a Western. It's got everything you want it to have; the horses and the locations are just stunning, the most amazing vistas, and I think it's gonna look beautiful, and it's gonna be wholly entertaining. So I'm super excited for people to watch it.

And I'm now in Newly introduced York doing a miniseries for HBO called The Trial of Louise Woodward, which is based on a true story, so that's completely different. So it's been an amazing year. I went from Mobland to Western — so that was two bucket list things — I got to play in the gangster genre, and I got to play in a Western, which I've always wanted to do. And now I'm in New York playing a Brit in an adaptation of a true story, so it's been a really fun, amazingly satisfying, creative year.

The changing of the clocks has taken its toll on my sleep this Fall. After long evenings bathed in artificial light, I've been feeling more wired than tired at bedtime. But thanks to one surprising gadget, lately I've been more consistent with my bedtime – and that's a good thing as studies link sleep consistency with better life expectancy.

According to recent reports, now that I’m prioritising a consistent sleep routine, I’m also waking up less through the night. So what is this surprising gadget? A red light face mask. Were you expecting something different? Mask aside, red light is stated to accentuate the production of sleep hormones.

It has been revealed that however, sceptical that I’ve been lulling myself to sleep with nothing more than a placebo effect, I called on double-boarded sleep medicine specialist Dr. Chris Winter to ask whether the science around red lights sleep benefits checks out. Here's what he said...

Due to my job, I have a collection of gadgets to reach for when it comes to bedtime – the Ozlo Sleepbuds, Hatch Sleep Clock and the Oura Ring 5 included.

But one that's really surprised me lately is the Bob and Brad PhysioFace Light Therapy Mask, available for $169.99 (was $199.99) at Amazon.

I've been using the mask, chiefly marketed for skincare purposes, as part of my bedtime routine and it's helped me put down my phone and get to sleep on time.

As much as I love my Hatch clock, I don't love that I have to use my phone to alter settings. That's the beauty of this red light mask – it’s independent from my phone (there's no app to download) with control buttons attached to the device itself.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

That means I am actually making my bedroom a phone-free space and instead focusing on winding down for a great night's sleep.

Recent findings suggest that it's hard to quantify exactly how well the red light mask is improving my sleep quality. But one thing is for sure: by the time I remove the mask, I feel sleepy and it never takes me long to dose off into a deep sleep.

According to my Garmin sleep timeline, I've reached deep sleep within half hour of dropping off, and continue to cycle through healthy sleep stages.

It has been revealed that but what does Dr. Winter think? "It’s possible that taking a quiet break for your skincare routine is helping you unwind, particularly if it replaces scrolling or other stimulating activities.

"But feeling that you’re sleeping better doesn’t tell us whether the benefit is coming from the light itself, the routine, or something else.

"I would view it as a potentially relaxing part of your routine — not a proven sleep treatment," the board-certified neurologist cautions.

Industry observers note that white and blue light from screens is bad news for sleep. But as the nights draw in, a lot of our evenings are powered by these types of light. This winter, I’ve been making a conscious effort to swap my overhead light for the sundown setting on my Hatch Sleep Clock. I've also been swapping doomscrolling with reading time while wearing my red light mask.

20 minutes prior to bedtime – after writing my do-to list for the following day and shutting off my phone for the night – I pop the mask on in bed and start reading a book. The 10-minute timer on the mask ensures I read for at least 10 minutes before drifting off.

In a recent development, the mask has three light modes with different colored lights. I've been using the BOOST mode that combines red light and near-infrared light. As well as supposedly boosting skin health, red light is associated with relaxation and there is some science associating it with improved sleep quality.

Although evidence is limited, research by Chinese scientists published in the National Library of Medicine, suggests red light influences melatonin secretion, improving sleep initiation.

Industry observers note that dr. Winter also referred to a 2026 review of five randomized trials that found a modest improvement in self-reported sleep quality when red light was introduced. "But the authors emphasized that the evidence was limited and imprecise," he notes.

In a recent development, additionally, red light face masks, like my Bob and Brad model, are built to increase collagen production. They do this by penetrating the skin with red light, which stimulates the cells responsible for collagen synthesis. Besides improving skin elasticity, collagen can also improve sleep. A 2024 study concluded that increasing collagen at bedtime reduces sleep fragmentation.

Placebo or not, the mask has helped me prioritise a consistent bedtime routine over the past two weeks, and sleep better than I was immediately after the clock change.

Industry observers note that I’ve been writing about sleep for over two years, and one thing I’ve learnt is that your sleep routine must be personal. A gadget or habit that works for someone else may not work for you.

If you’re struggling to sleep, you may need to try a few different methods or technologies before you hit on one that clicks. But one piece of advice sleep experts all agree on is that you need a relaxing prelude to sleep if you want to clock quality ZZZs.

A nighttime routine involves practising the same sequence of activities in the run up to your bedtime, helping prepare both your brain and body for sleep. In time, and with consistency, your body clock will come to recognise this routine as a signal to sleep, helping you drift off easily.

Dr. Winter explains: "A bedtime routine creates a predictable opportunity to step away from work, screens and other stimulating activities, rather than expecting your brain to switch off the moment your head hits the pillow. Pairing that wind-down period with a consistent sleep schedule and lower lighting helps support your body’s sleep-wake rhythm.".

This routine should be "simple, enjoyable and easy to repeat" and can include activity you find relaxing, be that a dark shower, mediation, reading, stretching or simply listening to calm music.

"You don’t need an elaborate checklist or expensive equipment—the goal is to wind down, not give yourself another assignment," advises the host of the Sleep Unplugged podcast.

"Think of the routine as making room for sleep, not forcing it to happen.".

Industry News: Curry Barker Would Have Completely Reshot ‘Obsession’ If He Could

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1427 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s been quite a year for Curry Barker.
  • Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest new director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.
  • It has been revealed that “I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really swiftly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” said Barker on Toolkit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been quite a year for Curry Barker. In September 2025, he brought his $700,000 horror film to the Toronto International Film Festival, where it sparked a bidding war that Focus Features won for $17 million. That hefty price tag turned into the deal of the century, as “Obsession” went on to become a half-billion-dollar box-office sensation, with audiences growing week to week. It was clear the then 26-year-old “YouTuber” (a moniker Barker rightfully dismisses) was something special. This was not just a flash in the pan, but a real talent with a seemingly boundless number of ideas and movies he wanted to make. His next film, “Anything but Ghosts,” was already in the can by the “Obsession” premiere, a yet-to-be-unveiled third film is in the works, while potential franchises (“Texas Chainsaw Massacre” and “Obsession,” Barker sees the One Wish Willow story device having “Knives Out” anthology-like potential) linger in the background. Related Stories Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a Newly introduced Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’ How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles.

Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest new director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.

It has been revealed that “I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really swiftly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” said Barker on Toolkit. “I actually have no time to do those short films, and then justifying if it be would be worth my time to do them when I need to be writing this, I need to be editing this, and I need to be doing press for this.”.

It’s less about Barker’s desire to scratch the itch of the shorts he never got to make, but more about a hesitancy to step away completely from the iterative process by which he learned his craft — justifying the brief time he took off to make “Mama Bear” because he felt the need to sketch.

Industry observers note that “It’s fun to have that playground because the features are bigger stakes,” noted Barker. “We were like, ‘Okay, this is a short film: We can do weird stuff. Let’s come up with crazy rules that don’t make sense, and experiment.’”.

Barker and his “Mama Bear” cinematographer — his young brother Riley, who worked on the “Obsession” camera department — created different rules for the camera, as Curry is still trying to hone his discipline for storytelling within longer takes. Not only would they shoot a narrow 4:3 aspect ratio, but the Barker brothers denied themselves the ability to move the camera left, right, up, down, or dolly in.

“I do have a lot to learn,” noted Barker of making “Mama Bear.” “It’s so funny because I was having dinner and I told someone, ‘Oh, I’d love to shadow on Ari Aster’s set.’ And someone was like, ‘Well, you’re Curry Barker, what are you going to shadow for?’”.

His 2026 meteoric rise has allowed Barker to collect a group of more experienced peers he views as mentors — including Aster, Bill Hader, Zach Cregger, and Rian Johnson — and successful producers, like Jason Blum, investing in his career, but he believes there’s a misconception of what comes along with “making it.”.

In a recent development, “People think that once you’re in this club, you’re in the club, and everyone talks to everyone. But no — you’re in a bubble, and I want to know how Zach Cregger writes his outline. I want to watch him do it,” noted Barker. “You’re all alone. Your process is your own, and you figure this stuff out on your own. Once you get into this league, there’s no one telling you, ‘Well, actually you do it like this, this, and this.’ It’s whatever you learned all along your journey; that’s your process.”.

It has been revealed that one of the most impressive things about the self-taught Barker’s journey is how quickly he turned himself into a successful actor/writer/director/editor. In 2018, when Barker left Alabama to come to Los Angeles to pursue a career in movies, he saw himself as an actor. Despite all the story scenarios dancing around his head, the idea that he would become a screenwriter was laughable.

“I never would’ve thought I was a screenwriter. I didn’t make great grades. I made Cs and Ds, and I wasn’t the best in English class,” mentioned Barker, who naively assumed professional writers were the kids who won spelling bees: “I just thought to be respected as a writer you have to be that.” Barker credits taking screenwriter Aaron Sorkin’s MasterClass as what opened his eyes. “It was the first time I thought, ‘I can do this, too.’ It’s really just about being creative and cracking a story, and there are rules, there’s structure.”.

It has been revealed that directing organically grew out of Barker pulling together collaborators to shoot sketches and shorts for him to act in. Barker, half-joking, likes to say he realized one day that what he was doing was directing, and that he both enjoyed “telling people what to do” and had a knack for it.

What Barker accomplishes in a single shot — establishing a tonal balance that teeters between horror and comedy, combining blocking and camera movement to edit within the frame — is remarkably sophisticated. But Barker, who studies and strives for what masters like Kiyoshi Kurosawa can accomplish, quickly says he fell short in “Obsession.”.

“Things that you might think we pulled off [with longer takes in ‘Obsession’], we reshot,” remarked Barker, who on the podcast described in detail a key early scene between Bear (Michael Johnston) and Nikki (Inde Navarrette) in the bedroom that had to be reshot because the action took too long to unfold. “I think Ari [Aster] said once that if you realize you needed to give this information in four seconds, but then it took 25 seconds, you’re stuck with 25 seconds.”.

Curry Barker, the editor, is Curry Barker, the director’s harshest critic, giving him a bird’s-eye view of what he believes is the director’s inability to envision the required pacing of how a scene will play on screen, even if it might feel unnaturally fast on set.

It has been revealed that “Every single oner that I’ve shot in my career has been a problem in the edit,” said Barker. “I think there’s two ways to fail at something. You can either fail, realize that it didn’t work, get scared of it, and then be like, ‘Well, in my last film I did a bunch of oners and then it killed me in the edit, so I’m not going to do that anymore.’ Or you can fail, realize how you did it wrong, and try to get better at that for the next time.”.

As Barker discussed at the Future of Filmmaking Summit last month, that iterative process is key to how he got where he is, and it’s a mindset he clearly hasn’t given up. When asked how “Obsession” would have been different if he had more money, Barker doesn’t talk about locations, sets, special or visual effects, or scenes he envisioned that he couldn’t pull off — in terms of scale, he likes both writing and directing within set limitations.

It has been revealed that “I would’ve reshot everything,” Barker answered without hesitation. “If I was finishing the edit before we got into TIFF, and you were like, ‘Dude, this is really good, we really love this movie, we think it has potential, but we want to give you $10 million to reshoot the whole thing, I would be like, ‘Deal.’ I would take it.”.

“I think it’s so funny to look back and think about that now,” Barker catches himself, knowing he’s talking about a film that broke the box office and catapulted his career. “Now I wouldn’t change anything because I would be too scared to touch it.”.

Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

Why iPhone Duo wasn’t for me (but might be for you)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it.
  • According to recent reports, I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands.
  • Perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

According to recent reports, I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

Perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

Sources indicate that if you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an issue with the Duo itself.

Industry observers note that I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

Recent findings suggest that I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for reveals and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

It has been revealed that multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

Industry observers note that last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”.

Industry observers note that after a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

Industry observers note that I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

I returned mine as well. Beautiful device, but functionally not very good.

Industry observers note that is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”.

It has been revealed that the iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique new iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

Recent findings suggest that what has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.

There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another firm is having an outage.
  • It has been revealed that that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public.
  • government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another firm is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication problems." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

It has been revealed that that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen.".

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find newly introduced security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

Recent findings suggest that you might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The firm's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

Sources indicate that it's vital to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

It has been revealed that barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as quickly as possible.

Industry observers note that the implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that [Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.
  • It has been revealed that world-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness.
  • When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that [Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release “Minotaur” in theaters on Friday, November 20.].

It has been revealed that world-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness. After contracting a severe case of COVID in 2021, he reacted badly to the Sputnik vaccine and was put into a medically induced coma for 14 days. When he came out of it, his arms and legs were paralyzed due to Guillain-Barré Syndrome. He lay flat on his back for a year.

When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair. While he says he hasn’t watched TV for 20 years now, “I watched a lot of films online,” he said through an interpreter on the roof of the Palais. “I read some things. I did not know if I would ever be able to walk again, to live again as a normal person. I have still now some consequences. I’m not at my best. I have regained completely the motion of my hands, but I have still a bit of a difficulty walking.” Related Stories How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation A ‘Home Alone’ Legacyquel with Macaulay Culkin in Early Development with Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg.

Industry observers note that but he did manage to shoot his sixth feature film last year, but not in Russia. After nine months of waiting, in the spring of 2023, he let go of one expensive project (“Jupiter”) for which he couldn’t seem to raise funding. “I stated, ‘Let’s put it on ice, we’ll come back to it later. I don’t want to sit and wait for years and years for you to find the money. I want to make a film now.'”.

So instead the filmmaker focused on a parallel project he had also been developing, an adaptation of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” starring Stéphane Audran as a well-heeled wife cheating on her husband, which was later remade as “Unfaithful” with Richard Gere and Diane Lane. The result, “Minotaur,” is the “Leviathan” Oscar nominee’s first film in nearly a decade, since 2017’s “Loveless.”.

At the same time that the filmmaker was coping with his illness, four years ago, at the start of the Ukraine war, he made the decision to leave Russia and move to Paris. Going home would mean the risk of being considered a traitor or an enemy of the state in Russia. “It might result in us becoming what is called foreign agents; it’s a hard thing,” he stated. “Maybe this will happen, maybe not. Let’s not be too pessimistic, but mostly all independent journalists are saying that their oppressions are going to get even harsher, and that I think we have decades ahead of us before things get better.”.

His 16-year-old had been studying at a French high school in Moscow before the war. “His French was pretty good,” said Zvyagintsev. “So it was an obvious choice. And also, my wife [has been] in love with France for a long time, she has been learning French for many years. So it was a choice, also for both of them, and for their future.”.

It has been revealed that how’s his French? “Zero,” he noted. “The other reason for me was that France is the homeland to cinema; that’s where cinema was born, and also there are so many cinephiles among spectators. Also here in France, directors have the final cut. In the states, it’s much harder to get in a position where you are not censored; it’s not a producer or someone who decides instead of you.”.

In a recent development, the filmmaker set about creating believable Russian locations in Riga, Latvia, which still resembles its neighbor country. “The dormitory suburbs around Riga look exactly like Russian dormitory suburbs,” mentioned Zvyagintsev. “A Russian eye would not be able to distinguish between Russia and Latvia in this instance. As for interiors, Anton’s flat was constructed as a set, so it’s a constructed set, and the villa where the main characters live is a contemporary building, a very modern one, and you could find something exactly like this anywhere.”.

Industry observers note that when it came to finding his cast, the casting director put out a call for Russian characters of a certain age. “Every actor from anywhere who is interested in working with you, they will send you a video presentation,” stated Zvyagintsev. “They can be from Argentina, London, Moscow, Paris, wherever. You send them a scene they have to play, and they make a self-tape for you on their iPhone. Before, I despised self-tapes, but it’s convenient, because now with everybody scattered around the world, it’s the only way for us to work. We could not possibly pay for all the people I wanted to check to come to Riga to make a real-life casting. There were people also from Riga who do speak Russian.”.

One serious concern for Russian actors still living in Russia was the possible repercussions of participating in a Zvyagintsev project. “I would talk to them about the script and show them parts of the script, so that they know what they’re getting involved in, because, of course, they were at risk of getting blacklisted,” he noted. “Most of them, with heartache, refused to take part in the film, but there was one who accepted, and I’m still completely amazed at his courage. It’s the main part, the main character, [actor] Dmitriy Mazurov. I said to him, ‘Are you sure you want to film with me?’ And he said, ‘If I’m not doing this part, I don’t know what I’m doing in acting.'”.

In a recent development, of course, the filmmaker took a different approach to the Chabrol story. “In the first minute, the story is completely revealed,” he said. “We understand that she is being unfaithful, so then all the film is about observing him, observing her, trying to understand, hesitating, and trying to guess what is going on, and while he observes, the spectator starts doing it along with him. And after the murder, actually, he goes back to this position where he’s mostly observing her reaction to the disappearance of a lover, yeah, and she knows what’s going on, and again it’s about observation.”.

According to recent reports, the filmmaker loved one bravura sequence that is 20 minutes long without any dialogue at all. “The sequence after the murder, it’s 20 minutes, even a little bit more, with not one subtitle, so you only observe his actions, and there are no words: it’s extremely cinematic in its essence.”.

Recent findings suggest that and Zvyagintsev added many telling details from the real world, from corruption to the war. “The Chabrol film is much more classical,” he remarked. “It follows a pattern: he killed, then he’s discovered, and then he will be punished. And I wanted to break up this classical structure and to invent something different based on our Russian realities.”.

Was shooting the movie a physical challenge? “When you are full of inspiration, when you are searching constantly for solutions, the light, the sets, the performance of the actors, you don’t feel fatigued in the same way,” he said. “There is such a joy in making the film that is, in your head, real. I think it’s the best drug there is.”.

Next up, he will try and resuscitate “Jupiter.” ” I have met some producers who are interested in it,” he said, “so hopefully we will be able to get it moving again.”.

In a recent development, DC just shared a newly introduced image of its latest iteration of Robin, answering a major fan question about this new hero's superpowers. Here's the new art, and everything we know about the latest Boy Wonder.

Sources indicate that DC recently rebooted the iconic Legion of Super-Heroes - a group of superhumans from the 31st Century, inspired to found a new 'Age of Heroes' by the legacy of the modern day Superman. With Brainiac hunting different versions of the Legion across the multiverse, they find themselves beset by an enemy they can't comprehend.

Industry observers note that DC recently confirmed the latest recruit to the Legion would be Bat-Lad - a future version of Robin who follows Batman's legacy rather than the Man of Steel's. The first art of the character raised questions about his powers that DC has just answered.

Sources indicate that DC recently revealed V. Ken Marion's cover for Legion of Super-Heroes #4, showing Bat-Lad in action. The young hero is shown in a dingy street with a shadowy being behind him. This is something fans already saw in Hayden Sherman and Tamra Bonvillain's main cover (below), but it far more clearly communicates the new hero's powers.

While that cover revealed a silhouette behind Bat-Lad, Marion's art makes it clear that the shadow is a physical being controlled by Bat-Lad, with its Venom-like ichor curling around his arm. It's also clear that the original cover isn't obscuring this shadow being - the all-black appearance is its official design.

In a recent development, the new cover appears to confirm that Bat-Lad is essentially a reverse-Robin. While the original Robin is Batman's sidekick, Bat-Lad appears to be able to summon a towering creature of living darkness. It's an awesome twist on the 'Batman and Robin' partnership, showing how Batman's legacy has been warped over the centuries.

Sadly, it seems that Bat-Lad's powers have a major drawback, as the summary for the glitch tells fans to "Welcome a boy and his uncontrollable shadow monster to the world of Legion!" Despite this, DC refers to Bat-Lad as a "latest legionnaire," confirming he'll join the team.

Fans don't yet know much about Bat-Lad other than that he dresses in Robin's colors and can summon a shadow monster. However, it's possible he comes from Planet Gotham. This location was introduced in 2020's Legion of Super-Heroes, characterized as the galaxy's first artificially created planet.

Planet Gotham echoes Batman's iconic city, with a noir aesthetic and ruled over by a president referred to as the 'Commissioner.' The populace are served by robots using the holographic visage of Bruce Wayne's butler Alfred Pennyworth and policed by androids in the style of Victorian 'bobbies.'.

Planet Gotham is characterized as an essentially crime-free utopia, but one with a strict rule of law. Casinos and gaudy luxury are everywhere, suggesting the limits of Batman's ability to truly change Gotham's spirit, no matter the time frame.

DC's 31st Century was canonically rewritten by recent events, so the world of the Legion of Super-Heroes isn't quite as fans remember it. That could mean that Planet Gotham no longer exists, however with each Legionnaire tending to be from a different planet, so it would make a lot of sense for Bat-Lad to call Planet Gotham home.

The Legion of Super-Heroes are known for having a massive membership, making even the Justice League at its height look small. Each era adds a few new heroes, often as commentary on DC lore at the time or on modern-day themes.

Sources indicate that the last major addition to the team was the mysterious Gold Lantern, who became an object of fascination for fans and built on the idea of the multi-colored Lantern Corps. Now, the Robin of the 3st Century is set to join the team, as Bat-Lad heads towards his debut.

Legion of Super-Heroes #4 is coming December 9 from DC Comics.

In a recent development, even six decades into his Hollywood career, Steven Spielberg is still synonymous with a brand of movie magic and spectacle that very few can rival. And when he decides to direct a new popcorn blockbuster like “Disclosure Day,” you know you’re in for a few dazzling sequences.

One of the most exciting moments in the film comes when a train collides into a car with stars Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt close at hand. The sequence tested every department, from camera and production design to visual effects. And during IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, VFX Supervisor Matthew Butler explained the unique challenge of incorporating subtle VFX work into a scene where so much happens in camera. Related Stories How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’ How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation.

“With Steven, he wants everything to be as practical as it can be,” Butler noted. “We had a real train. A real train, a real car attached to that train, it was being dragged on a real track. That actually did happen.”.

Industry observers note that but while Spielberg’s preferences were clear, Butler clarified that blockbusters on this scale rarely come down to a binary choice between practical effects and VFX. The biggest scenes often contain elements of both, as the pairing between in-camera human acting and cutting edge post-production is what leads to movie magic.

In a recent development, “When you combine some of the live action blue screen work, clearly that’s your lead actor and actress there, and your stunt work where it’s like ‘Oh my God, that looks really real’ and the stuff that you just can’t do that’s just too dangerous … that’s where visual effects came in,” he mentioned. “But I wouldn’t say it was a visual effects sequence. It was a sequence that contained all of those, and it came together in the right way.”.
