  • Goodnight Mommy definitely leans into the psychological horror aspect of an impostor mother much, much harder than Phony, but it’s just a deeper dive into the show’s darker implications (and, fair warning, this movie is dark).
  • According to recent reports, A woman identified only as Mother returns from having cosmetic surgery with her face totally enveloped in bandages, and her twin sons observe strange differences in her behavior that convince them she isn’t their real mother—she appears to ignore one of her sons completely, and disciplines them much more harshly than before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our relationships are foundational to our lives—our sense of safety and how we understand the world around us. When someone close to us suddenly, imperceptibly shifts, it can be unsettling, especially because you can’t be sure what’s changed or why. Those are the waters where Hulu’s Phony swims, delivering a perfectly pitched dramedy about a teenager (Sam Nivola) who emerges from a brief coma convinced that his mother (a pitch-perfect Connie Britton) has been replaced with a double. If you loved the series (and similar demonstrates) and you’re looking for more intriguing stories about doubles and impostors close to home, you should definitely watch Goodnight Mommy.

Goodnight Mommy definitely leans into the psychological horror aspect of an impostor mother much, much harder than Phony, but it’s just a deeper dive into the show’s darker implications (and, fair warning, this movie is dark).

According to recent reports, A woman identified only as Mother returns from having cosmetic surgery with her face totally enveloped in bandages, and her twin sons observe strange differences in her behavior that convince them she isn’t their real mother—she appears to ignore one of her sons completely, and disciplines them much more harshly than before. The boys also find clues that bolster their fears, including a photograph showing their mother posing with a woman dressed identically to her.

The boys’ attempts to force her to confess rapidly descend into a kind of madness, ultimately leading them to tie her to the bed in an effort to force her to admit she’s not their real mother. It all leads to a reveal as affecting as Phony’s ultimate explanation (albeit a lot more grim and violent). The film goes way harder than the series, but if you were totally into the premise, this is the more horrifying version you’ll want to see. The original film is German; there was a 2022 remake starring Naomi Watts, and while it's pretty good, the original is the right choice. Stream Goodnight Mommy on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

Sources indicate that looking for more impostor stories that dig into the psychological and emotional impact of suspecting someone has been replaced? Here are a few more movies that dig into the concept.

According to recent reports, the Hole in the Ground offers an inversion: A mother who becomes convinced that her son has been replaced by an impostor. Firmly in the supernatural horror genre, the story still plays the same game with the viewer: Is Sarah (Seána Kerslake) crazy, or has her son, Chris (James Quinn Markey), been replaced by a creature living in the woods near their home? It’s got the same disturbing energy as Sarah struggles with how much her son’s changed behavior is her own psychological projection and how much is clear evidence that he’s no longer the same person—or, possibly, even the same species. Stream The Hole in the Ground on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

Taking a slightly more literary approach (it’s based on a novella by Fyodor Dostoyevsky), The Double explores what happens if you find yourself replaced by a doppelgänger. Simon (Jesse Eisenberg) is a nonentity—ignored at work, lonely, and silently longing for the girl living across the street, Hannah (Mia Wasikowska). One day, a new employee named James appears at Simon’s job—and James looks exactly like Simon. But James is assertive, confident, and charming, sending Simon into a spiral. As the two versions slide into a battle for dominance, Simon finds himself turning to increasingly deranged moves to rid himself of the new and improved version of himself. If you loved the psychological implications that Phony explores, check out The Double. Stream The Double on Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

On one level, Denis Villeneuve’s 2013 film is about a college professor named Adam (Jake Gyllenhaal) who discovers an actor named Anthony who looks exactly like him (also played by Gyllenhaal). When he tracks his double down, their lives merge in messy ways, ending in tragedy and one of the most striking (and confusing) final shots in cinema history. On another level, Enemy is a deft trick, exploring someone’s subconscious using dream logic and misdirection. If the best part about Phony was the disorienting sense that a secret just under the surface will explain everything, Enemy is the perfect choice. Stream Enemy on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re looking for a deeper, crazier, and more terrifying story about doubles, Andrzej Żuławski’s 1981 film is a terrific choice. Inspired in part by his own feelings in the wake of a painful divorce, the story follows Mark (Sam Neil), a spy who returns to West Berlin at the height of the Cold War only to find out his wife, Anna (Isabelle Adjani), has been having an affair and wants a divorce. But Anna’s behavior becomes increasingly strange, and then Mark meets their son’s teacher, Helen, who looks just like Anna. And that’s before Anna kind of ... grows a replacement Mark from a tentacled creature kept in her bathroom (and that’s just the beginning of how weird this movie gets), resulting in two doubles. How much of the film is meant literally and how much simply represents the trauma of romantic betrayal and divorce is up to you, but Possession will definitely leave a mark. Stream Possession on Shudder, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Obsession looks at the Doppelgänger Effect from a different perspective. Cliff Robertson plays Michael Courtland, a wealthy businessman whose wife (Geneviève Bujold) and young daughter, Amy (Wanda Blackman), are kidnapped in 1959. When he follows police advice against delivering the ransom, both appear to be killed in an explosion. Courtland spends the next 16 years hating himself, until he encounters a young woman, Sandra (also Bujold), who looks almost exactly like his late wife. He works to make Sandra look as much like his wife as possible, and eventually proposes—but then Sandra is kidnapped in precisely the same way as his wife and daughter sixteen years before. This all leads to a head-spinning series of reveals and a twist that echoes the Hitchcock classic Vertigo. Rent Obsession on Prime Video.

In a recent development, I began working on dettato about 10 months ago, but scrapped what I had in about April. The reason why was that I treated AMT as a data problem - but in reality, the bottleneck is architecture. There are a lot of parellels that you can draw for OMR (first model i made) and AMT. both traditionally were tackled early on using algorithms. later, in both fields they plugged in giant LLM components. These models would naturally become overfit to synthetic data, since globally the problems of AMT and OMR become different than if you treat it locally. But, for both you can reframe it as a local problem. For OMR, using a detector model. For AMT, a pitch-lane model.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, right now the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and people who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

The SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

Industry observers note that it comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple indicates the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

The majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

If your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

Sources indicate that yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Recent findings suggest that black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stocks were slammed on Friday, closing out a brutal week for markets as the much-hyped Anthropic IPO caused investors to take profits on the artificial intelligence-led rally rather than revive it.
  • Industry observers note that the tech-heavy Nasdaq shed 5.28% to close at 22,617.73.
  • The Nasdaq-100 plummeted 5.6% and entered a bear market on an intraday basis, down 20% from its recent high.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stocks were slammed on Friday, closing out a brutal week for markets as the much-hyped Anthropic IPO caused investors to take profits on the artificial intelligence-led rally rather than revive it. The Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year, and the S&P 500 entered correction territory alongside the Dow Jones Industrial Average.

Industry observers note that the tech-heavy Nasdaq shed 5.28% to close at 22,617.73. The index was down 2.7% year to date. The broad market S&P 500 dropped 3.7% to end at 6,910.39, while the blue-chip Dow fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33. Both the S&P 500 and Dow moved 10% below their closing records.

The Nasdaq-100 plummeted 5.6% and entered a bear market on an intraday basis, down 20% from its recent high.

It has been revealed that anthropic lost 8.5%, giving back a large chunk of its 17% jump in its Nasdaq debut Thursday and pressuring the broader AI trade. Chipmakers Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia slid more than 13% and around 14%, respectively. Nvidia saw selling pressure increase after Reuters reported that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring possible accounting issues at the company. It also recorded its longest weekly losing streak since the 2008 financial crisis. Micron Technology dropped almost 14%.

Those declines in tech built on the losses seen in Thursday's horrid session, where the major averages each losing more than 2%, and the Dow closing below the key 50,000 level for the first time since June.

Recent findings suggest that "This is not just a valuation-driven correction. It's becoming broader," mentioned Massimo Santicchia, head of U.S. equities at Procyon. "Right now, it's definitely risk-off.".

The losses are alarming investors who were hopeful that Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's IPO would revive enthusiasm for the AI trade. Now, the market looks to be on the cusp of a true capitulation after getting roiled in recent weeks with a series of negative headlines. Signs of moderation in the capital expenditures splurge, Democratic wins in the 2026 midterms and Jensen Huang's ouster at Nvidia all raised questions about the future of the AI buildout.

On top of that, the potential for more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve is spooking traders as well.

Investors hid out in defensive areas of the market, with retailers such as Walmart and Costco as well as others like Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble seeing gains. Walmart gained more than 1%, while Costco, Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble each rose around 1%.

"The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth," noted Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners.

For the week, the Dow fell 8%, notching its worst weekly performance since March 2020. The Nasdaq finished down about 10%, also posting its largest one-week pullback in more than six years. The S&P 500 decreased 8.6%, seeing its worst week since April 2025 in the wake of President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs announcement.

It has been revealed that the three leading U.S. indexes experienced a massive sell-off on Friday.

The S&P 500 dropped 3.7% to close at 6,910.39, while the Nasdaq Composite plummeted 5.28% to 22,617.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33.

All three major averages were trading below their 200-day moving averages on Friday, and BTIG believes more turmoil could be ahead.

"Generally speaking once something is below a 200 DMA, the risk is to the downside," noted Jonathan Krinsky, the firm's chief market technician.

Thursday marked the sixth consecutive day of declines for the S&P 500, and Krinsky found that over the last 30 years, there are only three prior instances of six-day losing streaks that close below the 200-day moving average but not by more than 3%.

"The 'slightly' good news is that all three saw SPX higher five days later. The not so good news is that all of them saw meaningful downside after that small pop," he said.

When assessing Thursday's performance, Wolfe Research found that the broad market index's "violent" reversal after its attempt to move back to its 200-day moving average at the open was succeeded by the "worst breadth reading" since last December, seeing decliners outnumber advancers by 12:1.

It has been revealed that "Broken trends and deteriorating momentum remain significant headwinds," wrote technical analyst Rob Ginsberg in a Thursday note. "The bulls need to mount a powerful defense here to stabilize the market and begin reversing the broader deterioration.".

In a recent development, the national average for regular gasoline fell to $3.69 a gallon on Friday, down from $3.72 on Thursday, according to AAA. Prices are still about 59 cents higher than a year ago.

The drop comes ahead of Thanksgiving next week, with 73 million people expected to take road trips.

"It's possible the national average will drop another 15 cents by next Thursday and avoid setting a newly introduced record," according to AAA's post.

Brent ​crude futures, the international benchmark, were up 0.64% to $92.57 a barrel on Friday, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for December rose 0.93% to settle at $83.98 a barrel.

Humana shares rose 3% after TD Cowen upgraded the healthcare services organization to buy from hold, raising the price target to $485, implying a 28% upside from the stock's Thursday close of $380.

"Taking into account 2026 performance, 2027 Medicare Advantage benefit design and 2028 Stars results, we see a relatively clear path towards a meaningful step-up in 2027 EPS growth and more than $40 EPS in 2028," the bank remarked in its note.

Adjusted EPS estimates for 2026, 2027, and 2028 remain unchanged at $9.51, $18.41, and $40.42, respectively.

Anthropic was the most-traded single stock by Vanguard's self-directed retail traders on Thursday, underscoring the buzz among mom-and-pop investors around the artificial intelligence leader's historic IPO.

Just about 0.2% of Vanguard's self-directed investors bought Anthropic on Thursday, which was its first day on the public market. These investors bought a median of 20 shares or roughly $1,950.

Vanguard said about around out of every 10 Anthropic buyers were men. By comparison, men account for 55% of Vanguard's investor base.

To be sure, Vanguard noted a higher percentage of its base traded SpaceX during its public market debut session in June.

Anthropic jumped 17% in trading on Thursday after it went public. But the stock has dropped nearly 10% in afternoon trading Friday, which is its first full day on the market.

BTIG's chief market technician Jonathan Krinsky in an appearance on CNBC's "The Exchange" Friday pointed to technicals that make him think the sell-off isn't over just yet.

He specifically noted Apple, the largest stock by market cap, which is only down by 3% from its 2026 highs earlier this month. "When the S&P has been down at least 8% or more, when it's made its final bottom, the median drawdown for Apple has been 23%," he remarked. "It would be historically unprecedented to see a final bottom on the S&P with Apple where it is right now.".

He added that 50% of the S&P 500's stocks are above their 50-day moving average, a level that is higher than a number closer to below 40% — or even 20% — when durable bottoms hit.

Krinsky did note, though, that relief for semiconductors may be coming, as the group is retreating to levels that it last traded at in early April when the group started to surge higher. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) in late trading Friday was at levels it last closed below on April 9.

Anthropic debuted with a 17% advance on Thursday, starting off on the wrong foot as its performance came up short when compared with the day-one gains from other notable IPOs since last year.

The day-one moves of Circle, Figma, Cerebras and SpaceX all outdid Anthropic's, with Figma seeing the biggest jump at 250%.

Anthropic shares gave back much of that advance on Friday, falling more than 12% in afternoon trading.

According to recent reports, president Donald Trump mentioned on Friday that he wants to stop U.S. companies from building data centers in other countries.

It has been revealed that "We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference. He added that companies would face tremendous penalties for building data centers abroad. "We want them to build it here.".

According to recent reports, he added that he is concerned about U.S. companies building in China instead. "We're not allowing that to happen," he said.

Industry News: Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3343 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.
  • It has been revealed that advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated.
  • Recent findings suggest that the sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.

It has been revealed that advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

Recent findings suggest that the sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

Sources indicate that in the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

Recent findings suggest that “It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn swiftly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Industry observers note that miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký.

Sources indicate that during totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Industry observers note that druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

Industry observers note that an image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”.

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Václav Široký and Miloslav Druckmüller.

In a recent development, despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

Industry observers note that to observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most key processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

Recent findings suggest that that’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

In a recent development, the European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”.

According to recent reports, the error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” claims Habbal.

It has been revealed that capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.).

Industry observers note that the human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

In a recent development, to create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

Industry observers note that the teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

Recent findings suggest that “Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký.

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller notes with a grin. “It’s perfect.”.

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

It has been revealed that as the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

It has been revealed that twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký.

Industry observers note that those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

According to recent reports, “That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

Sources indicate that the optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek.

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”.

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

According to recent reports, with just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

It has been revealed that the crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

It has been revealed that “The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller indicates. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”.

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký.

It has been revealed that but for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller claims.

Sources indicate that who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Sales are accurate at the time of publication, but prices and inventory are always subject to change.

Sources indicate that not every Black Friday or Cyber Monday deal is as sweet as it seems. With electronics and tech in particular, you could be buying last year's model that has actually been on sale since the summer—and was maybe a better price a few months ago. Here’s how to avoid impulse buying a misleading Black Friday “deal” and make sure you’re getting the best bang for your buck.

When you see products like food, clothes, or home goods with a massive "Black Friday" or "Cyber Monday" tag slapped on them, it's probably safe to take advantage of that deal. Chances are it's the same exact product you'd find on other days of the year. The same can’t be mentioned for a TV, laptop, and other tech deals, where the product itself is constantly being upgraded.

Because tech is always evolving, and retailers want to move inventory before upcoming models come out, electronics are especially susceptible to a practice known as "price anchoring." That's when retailers mark up prices in the weeks leading up to Black Friday, before "slashing" those prices back down, giving the appearance of a deal that isn't really a deal at all. Still, when you see that marked-up number, aka the "price anchor," you might get tricked into thinking you're saving money when you're not. There's also the false sense of urgency that gets created. It's second nature to assume that anything labeled "deal" won’t last long—even when this so-called deal price has actually been going on since the summer.

According to recent reports, price anchoring isn't even unique to Black Friday. The nonprofit Consumers’ Checkbook tracked prices at 25 major retailers over 33 weeks in 2022 and found that more than half the items tracked were offered at false discounts every week or almost every week. Less common, but also worth noting, is a known practice of "derivative" or retailer-exclusive models produced specifically for the holiday shopping season. These versions often feature cheaper components, fewer features, or lower specifications than their regular counterparts. A 55-inch TV from a reputable brand might look identical to the year-round model, but it could have a lower refresh rate, inferior panel technology, or fewer HDMI ports.

Sources indicate that in the same vein, that "amazing deal" on a laptop might come with last year's processor, or a smartphone that's about to be replaced. The glitch isn't that the tech is an older model, but again, it's that it probably has been at this low a price, or lower, since the summer. Alternatively, some deeply discounted electronics are refurbished units or open-box returns that have been repackaged. Again, while this isn't necessarily a bad thing, impulse buyers may not fully realize what they're buying.

In a recent development, the key phrasing here is impulse buying. Events like Black Friday are psychologically engineered to trigger impulse purchases. Limited-time offers, countdown clocks, and "while supplies last" warnings create artificial urgency. When you're caught up in the moment, it's easy to convince yourself you need a new tablet, smartwatch, or gaming console, even if you hadn't considered buying one before.

Recent findings suggest that to avoid a low-key scam, do your research. The easiest way to tell that you’re getting the correct product is by checking the model or serial number. And with online shopping, finding and double-checking those numbers is quick and easy. In addition, don't just compare prices—compare specs. Look at processor speeds, RAM, storage capacity, screen resolution, refresh rates, and connectivity options. A $300 laptop isn't a deal if a slightly more expensive model offers significantly better performance that will last longer.

Recent findings suggest that if you do see a deal that catches your eye, it could pay to wait. Cyber Monday, post-Christmas sales, and even January clearances often feature electronics deals that rival or beat Black Friday prices, all without the famous chaos and pressure. Then again, you risk more “out-of-stock” results if you wait, so the risk is up to you, depending on the popularity of the item you’re eyeing (and how badly you want it).

The bottom line: Don’t fall victim to a falsely advertised lower-quality product, and do a little research to find actually good deals ahead of time.

According to recent reports, yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Industry observers note that yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

The offer came following the closing of Skydance’s purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery, as the company seeks $6 billion in savings. The merger puts CBS News and CNN under the same corporate umbrella.

At CBS News, the buyout was accepted by employees across the news division, with the London bureau among the most impacted, sources familiar with the aims noted. Some staffers on 60 Minutes also took the buyout, although none were in key lead editorial roles, according to a source. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that you can cancel your Prime subscription via web browser by first logging into your Amazon account. Amazon has a Cancel Your Prime Membership button on its support page to launch the process, or you can follow the steps detailed on Amazon's page:.

Head to Amazon.com in your web browser.

Hover over the Accounts & Lists menu on the top-right of the window, then select the Prime Membership option.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

Note that Amazon requires a bunch of clicks to finalize your cancellation, giving you lots of “opportunities” to change your mind.

Open the Amazon Shopping app on your mobile device.

Click the three horizontal lines on the bottom right.

Under Shop by Category, select Prime.

On the top bar, slide all the way to the end and select Help.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

As mentioned, closing your account will immediately end your access. Amazon also offers you the option to pause your benefits and billing temporarily instead of canceling them completely. Either way, your Amazon account is still active—you simply won’t have Prime benefits.

Finally, if you have other subscriptions connected to your Prime account, those will end when your billing is up. And if you signed up for Prime through the Android mobile shopping app or the Prime Video Android app, you’ll have to go through Google Subscription to manage your membership.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the world has been waiting to play Grand Theft Auto VI, and the video game is finally here. Music, of course, is integral to all of it. There’s a soundtrack full of stars — the 34-track release, which is out today, features Travis Scott, Keith Richards, Dua Lipa, Arca, and more. In addition to that, there is a massive one-day festival inspired by the game, taking place in Miami on Nov. 21, with headliners Cardi B, Metro Boomin, and Justice, who also put together the game’s score.

Once you start playing, there’s even more music to discover through the game’s radio stations and celebrity DJ hosts. Here are some of the best music moments and surprise cameos from the biggest video game of the year.

In a recent development, the game is full of celebrity guest DJs, which Rockstar began sharing a few weeks back. There’s Cocoteo FM hosted by Bad Bunny and RaiNao, Back Country Radio hosted by Morgan Wallen and Lana Del Rey, and Radio La Ola with Gloria and Emilio Estefan, plus tons more. But one that may surprise people is Stockyard FM, featuring two DJs named Victoria and Harrison — better known as PinkPantheress and the Dare. Victoria and Harrison are their real names, and their radio station is dedicated to experimental, left-of-center pop, electronica, and indie sleaze.

One of the GTA VI radio stations, Radio La Ola, plays homage to Latin classics from over the decades. But one hugely surprising one is “Sopa de Caracol,” a massive but somewhat forgotten hit from the Nineties by Honduran band Banda Blanca. The inclusion made headlines in Central America, with the lead singer Pilo Tejada saying he was honored to have his voice reach fresh parts of the world.

Psych-rock band King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard is featured on the soundtrack: They’re one of several artists on the collaboration “Flower in a Hurricane,” which also earned them their first Billboard 100 entry. But that’s not the only place you can find them: Gizz fans noticed that throughout several parts of the game, you can hear snippets of what appear to be demos from the band, woven into the score. On Reddit, diehards have been pointing these out and playing guessing games as they wonder what projects these might be from.

In a recent development, we’ve known that the French electronic duo Justice composed the original score for the game, but the official album won’t be out until Dec. 11. We’re getting to hear some of what they came up with the release of the game but there’s still more to come, including an anticipated collaboration with the Weeknd. The duo have since said this is the “first and last” video game they’ll ever score.

According to recent reports, the soundtrack, which dropped on Nov. 19, is packed, featuring 34 songs by some surprising artists and stars. There’s new music from Travis Scott, the Fuerza Regida track “Suzuki,” which is charting in 15 countries, and there are also songs from Keith Richards, Kali Uchis and Helado Negro, and more. A lot of the music was inspired directly by Miami, which you can hear in new tracks from artists like JT.

Sources indicate that artists are getting into the game, too. Tinashe delighted fans with a hilarious livestream playing for the first time. The stream captured her making an epic getaway by flying an airplane and hysterically crashing it into the ground, then running out of ammo in a shootout. “I have no bullets!” she screams. “Holy shit, I’m going to have to beat the fuck out of them myself.” After several days of sold-out reveals in the U.K., Noah Kahan stayed up late and wreaked havoc in Vice City while his wife was asleep.

In a recent development, the world lost D’Angelo back in 2025, but his legacy lives on in Vice City. GTA VI players discovered that an unreleased track called “Kamakazi,” as confirmed by D’Angelo collaborator DJ Dojah, is one of the songs you can hear on the radio station Worldwide FM. D’Angelo’s “Lady” also plays on the in-game Honey FM channel, which is hosted by Chilli and T-Boz of TLC.

Sources indicate that while the creators of the game spent a ton of time adding interesting radio stations and track to the GTA VI universe, there is plenty of love for pop stars and major pop hits. Dua Lipa appears on the soundtrack, but the radio stations also feature plenty of pop girlies: There’s Chappell Roan’s “Hot To Go!,” Charli XCX’s “Good Ones,” and Addison Rae’s “Fame Is a Gun,” just to name a few, which players can blast while driving through Vice City.

#62639. Latest Update: Apple among the companies facing pressure from US senators over ‘nudify’ apps [U: Apple, TTP respond]

Latest Update: Apple among the companies facing pressure from US senators over ‘nudify’ apps [U: Apple, TTP respond]

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1500 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps.
  • Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable customers to generate nonconsensual nude images.
  • According to the updated rules, apps that allow consumers to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps. Here are the details.

Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable customers to generate nonconsensual nude images.

According to the updated rules, apps that allow consumers to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.

Apple also warns that apps used primarily for pornographic content or the objectification of real people may be removed from the App Store without notice.

While definitely well-intended, Apple’s changes came amid growing reports of AI-powered nudify apps, which easily allow users to generate nonconsensual intimate images.

Two months before these changes, Apple removed an app that allowed customers to create pornographic deepfakes of real people after WIRED reached out for comment, which in turn came one month after San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu demanded that Apple and Google remove several nudify apps from their app stores.

Apple also removed several apps following investigations by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), which published reports in January and April revealing that such apps were widely available on the App Store, sometimes even appearing in sponsored search results.

Throughout these investigations, Apple has maintained that nudify apps have always been prohibited under its App Review Guidelines, and that it proactively rejects and removes apps that violate its policies, including those flagged through user reports.

Apple, of course, is not alone in this challenge, with Google facing similar criticism over their availability on the Play Store, and Meta coming under scrutiny for allowing developers to advertise these apps on Facebook and Instagram, as highlighted in the WIRED report mentioned above.

Which brings us to today’s report from The Guardian.

According to The Guardian’s exclusive report, “three Senate Democrats sent letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms.”.

Sources indicate that A trio of US Senators say Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. They also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

The senators, namely Ron Wyden of Oregon, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Ben Luján of Newly introduced Mexico, claim that in addition to failing to remove these apps, the companies may actually be profiting from their distribution and promotion.

Commenting on the letter, both Google and Meta remarked they prohibit such apps or their promotion and work to detect and remove violations from their platforms, broadly echoing what Apple has repeatedly stated when reached for comment in the past over these same concerns.

However, Wyden’s office argues that simply reaffirming, or in Apple’s case, updating these policies, means little if the companies continue to struggle to enforce them.

In a recent development, keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, said that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he added.

In its latest investigation, published just last month, TTP found 135 apps capable of generating nude or pornographic imagery on the App Store and the Play Store, using accounts registered to 13-year-old boys.

Additionally, researchers found that even accounts configured with parental controls were able to download these apps without requiring parental approval.

Despite Apple and Google removing the apps identified in the investigation, The Guardian noted that these apps continued to work on devices where they had already been installed.

Now, Senator Wyden warns that Congress may need to step in if the companies fail to do a better job of cracking down on these apps.

To read The Guardian’s full report, follow this link.

Industry observers note that update, 8:40 p.m. ET: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple stated:.

Industry observers note that “We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for consumers. A number of the apps in the TTP report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities. We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process — a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch. We previously removed 28 of the apps referenced in this report before it was shared with us and have taken action on the remaining apps found to violate our rules. The report also relies on testing from older software that does not reflect current Apple safety features, including expanded protections for teens and parental controls in Screen Time that give families the ability to block kids and teens from downloading apps rated above their age.”.

Expanding on the safety features mentioned in its statement, Apple noted that teens aged 13 through 17 now have certain protections enabled by default, including web content filters, even if their parents haven’t configured any restrictions, and pointed to ⁠this support article for more information.

The firm added that children under 13 are required to use Child Accounts, and that the report relied on its previous 17+ age rating system, which was replaced last year with a more granular system that includes 13+, 16+, and 18+ ratings.

Just curious. Why doesn't someone from Apple try out the app before approving it, rather than approving it and waiting until people complain? I know there are many thousands of apps on the App store. But given that Apple makes money off most of these apps, it could surely afford to hire a staff charged with reviewing submitted apps to ensure compliance with the App store's guidelines and requirements before making them available in the App store. What am I missing here?

Apple also noted that in its report, TTP counted apps depicting people in swimwear or lingerie, which the company said does not constitute nudification or, in itself, violate its guidelines.

As for parental controls, Apple explained that, although apps that exceed a child’s configured age restrictions won’t appear in curated App Store sections, they can still be found through search, allowing children to request permission to download them through Ask to Buy. Without parental approval, the download remains blocked.

Apple added that Ask to Buy is supposed to require parental approval even for purchases made using gift card balances, including subscriptions. The firm remarked that if a purchase didn’t trigger an approval request, that would be unexpected behavior, and that it is investigating further.

It has been revealed that update, November 19, 4:00 p.m. ET: In response to Apple’s statement, TTP director Katie Paul reached out to 9to5Mac with the following comment:.

Apple’s statement on nudify apps sidesteps important complications and leaves out key context. The company states it prohibits nudify apps but doesn’t address how its age rating system for apps contributes to the problem. TTP has shown how Apple relies on information provided by app developers to set age ratings—a self-reporting system that allows many nudify and pornographic apps to be misleadingly labeled a suitable for minors. Apple also continues to talk about removing nudify apps from the App Store, without mentioning that apps that are “removed” continue to be fully functional on people’s phones.

There are many questions about Apple’s policy on nudify apps that the statement fails to address. Apple has adopted a limited definition of “nudify.” The company defines nudify apps as capable of showing someone naked, not stripping them down to a bikini or lingerie. But the company also claims it bans “creepy” and “nonconsensual intimate imagery.” What if an app is used to depict a woman in a bikini without her consent? We have asked Apple to clarify that and have not heard back.

As for Apple’s comment that TTP relied on “older software,” that may refer to the fact that Apple rolled out latest child safety features in the fall. Our research was conducted in summer 2026. But many of Apple’s new features pertain to parent-supervised accounts on Apple, which have to be set up by a parent. Apple relies entirely on parents to go out of their way to locate and enable these settings. This raises obvious questions about how many people actually do this.
